en: The Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Campū: The First Campū, the First Supplement.
Obeisances to Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Ramaṇa; obeisances to Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya; O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, along with Sanātana and Rūpa!
O Gopāla, O Raghunātha, O Lord of Vraja attained by [the devotees], protect me!
[1] Thus, having suddenly engraved this with a great inner brilliance born from its commencement, the following is inscribed:
what is this? It is the sequential recollection that has manifested of my chosen deity and of the assembly of his devotees, who are distinguished by the compassion I have sought from them.
Or rather, is it [the worship] of my chosen deity alone? Or is it that [deity] as qualified [by others]?
Yes, yes; according to the tantras, all three of these are obtained independently.
In this regard, first of all, I shall initially set forth [the following]:
here, the word "śrī" (glory) and various other words are to be supplied in the *anuṣṭubh* meter or in another meter wherever they have not been provided previously or subsequently,
and in those places they should be joined together.
[2] For example: "O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, most blessed by name! O foremost of all!
O Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya!"
O you who bestow all auspiciousness and are worthy of praise; O you whose name is Śrī Rūpa, eternally accompanied by the worshiped Śrī [Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī],
may you be placed upon my head.
O Śrī Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, enriched by the exalted status of a great venerable teacher;
O Śrī Raghunātha Dāsa,
renowned as the very abode of the Name and pierced by the weight of supreme devotion!

O Śrīvallabha! O refuge of my father’s feet, which are joined to me through the merit accumulated in previous births that was difficult to attain! You are the locus of such names as Bhūgarbha and others, whose ears are adorned with the glorious descriptions of perfected beings moving among the trustworthy.
Or rather: O Śrīvallabha, beloved of all, who follows those who follow the trusted attendants of Śrī Raghunātha—
protect me!
Come as the protector of me with the shade of your own feet,
so that you may quickly proclaim the playful bliss of the enemy of Kaṃsa,
and, shining forth as an ally, act as a dear friend.
No other fortunate person exists like him;
thus, perceiving even a second [person], I create him as Śrī-Kṛṣṇa.
"Śrī" here refers to Rādhā;
for she is unimpeded in the sense of being the primary Śrī who is to be established [as the subject].

Furthermore, the word "Kṛṣṇa" used immediately thereafter is conventionally established here as denoting the Sound-Brahman (śabda-brahman), the hidden Supreme Brahman (gūḍha-para-brahman), and the Son of Nanda.
By this, the meaning “Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti) called Śrī Rādhā,” is established.
Regarding the word *kṛṣṇa*: the word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth, and *ṇa* denotes bliss (*nirvṛti*).
The supreme Brahman, which is the unity of those two, is designated as Kṛṣṇa.

Thus, the word *kṛṣṇa*, whose usage is known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), refers here primarily to that [Supreme Being] by virtue of being a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) preceded by its etymological derivation (*yoga*). The word *bhūḥ* is formed from the verbal root with the suffix *kvip* expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*);
and like a word denoting an abstract state, it bears the meaning of the verbal root alone.
And here the meaning of the verbal root is "attracting" (*ākarsana*);
that itself is clearly the attracting of those whose minds have attained [the goal] through being authoritative (*āpta*).

Consequently, since those two are understood to be distinct entities, their union (*yoga*)—like that of two beloveds—is indeed oneness; thus, the bliss joined with that is the bliss that attracts all, and for this very reason, it is "unfailing" (*amanda*).
Regarding the phrase "the Supreme Brahman":
it is well known that the Supreme Brahman has a human form;

furthermore, because its conventional meaning is underpinned by its yogic (etymological) sense, the power of that word denotes none other than the Śrī-Nandanandana—thus its specific identity is established.
This is what is being expressed and re-expressed.
Therefore, this repetition serves to apply the logical reasoning for the very purpose of cultivating the specific nature of that [consciousness].
Thus: "consciousness."
“He is the illuminator of all;
his own nature is the substratum of all by virtue of being the essence of existence.
And this nature has been realized by the wise.

"Because of the *Tāpanīya* and *Nāndī* [Upaniṣads] stating, 'To Kṛṣṇa, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss (sac-cid-ānanda) and whose actions are untainted,' and because of the concluding verse in the *Brahma-stava* of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, 'In you alone, whose body is eternal bliss and consciousness'—
thus [he is called] 'possessing an eternal form'."

“He who exists together with that which is eternal (*sanātana*), ever-present (*sadātana*), and whose form is perfectly defined even for those experiencing His own nature; by whom the minds and hearts of His devotees are led;
[He who is called] Gopāla, Raghunātha, Āpta, and Vrajavallabha.”
O beloved of the excellent cowherds of Vraja, who have attained [prosperity] through those Raghus among the cowherds who are swift, and those leaders whose fame is celebrated as preeminent!

Alternatively, [the name] may be understood through the *nānārthavarga* (section on multiple meanings) as follows: "The term *laghu* is desired in three senses: as 'cowherd' (*gopāla*), as 'light' (*alpa*), and as 'lord' (*nātha*). Thus, it is an address to him who is both the light cowherd and the lord.
"Beloved of the assembly of the trustworthy" (*āptavrajavallabha*) means: "the beloved of the assembly of the trustworthy, that is, of his own circle of kinsmen;
possessing true radiance unattainable by others.
Now, I shall also perform the third *sambhṛtī* rite:
"He is Śrī-Kṛṣṇa. Here, "Śrī" refers to Rādhā, who is the most excellent among those most dear to Him; therefore, by virtue of being united with Her, He is unadulterated in His sweet pastimes.
O you who are the incarnation of devotion known as Kṛṣṇacaitanya,
who have descended by having attained identity with Him;
O you who are present together with the two most devoted and excellent devotees in the forms of Sanātana and Rūpa.
"Protect me, who am dear to that Vraja which was obtained— attained through the two of you, Gopāla and Raghunātha, who are likewise excellent devotees; and come to be my protector."
Now, the indication of the text:
[5] Thus, having established the auspicious invocation, the subject matter is considered:
that nectar of the final doctrine which has been gathered by me in the *Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*.

That very thing is relished by one who possesses the discernment of poetic creation and the capacity for aesthetic appreciation. (JGc 1.1.2) Such as I am, I fashion my mind through the observation of poetry in such a way that when the great behold it, they will see a jewel set within gold. (JGc 1.1.3)

This pair of *campū*s, consisting of three parts each—prior and subsequent—is equal in extent to separate individual works; let them be examined by the virtuous as they desire. [Anuṣṭubh] For the delight of the cowherds, the followers of the illustrious Gopāla.
Let this work, known by the name *Gopāla-campū*, be complete in every respect.
[Upagīti] Although the glory of those residing in Śrī-Gokula has long been hidden from view, nevertheless, the multitude of their manifestations shines forth before us; may it be victorious! [Udgīti]
[6] There is, it is said, a forest named Vṛndāvana, as fortunate as if it were the very fortune of the Goddess of the Earth;
for behold, though it is but a forest, it is capable of protecting the entire world.
Even the wind that blows there, by its mere presence, surpasses the state of being "wind" through the power of its swiftness.
Though it always bestows the three goals of human life without restraint, it ever excludes liberation;
though it possesses even the scent of a connection with those bound for emancipation, it becomes the cause of the persistent bondage of its own fetters;
and though it always grants devotion to the Lord of the Satyaloka, it never at any time bestows devotion to Him.

Having considered that even what was not yet fully realized within the self by Brahmā was desired as birth, he thereby understood it to be the supreme realization; thus, he demonstrates the undertaking of a majesty exalted by its own inherent benefit.

In this way, although the meaning appears contradictory—like the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra*—due to the confusion arising from the practice of the profound (*gahana-caryā*), he transforms it through its ultimate resolution into a state of complete consistency.
In him, even in the absence of poetry by other poets, poetry will be held in high esteem;
and in him alone is the supreme nobility of essence perceived.
For he, the glorious son of Nanda, who has repeatedly descended for the sake of the welfare of all, is the mountain that forever supports every festival of bliss for everyone.
[7] And here there is also a verse by Śrī Śuka, which is a cause for the wonder of bliss:
"O King, upon seeing Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, and the sandy banks of the Yamunā, the supreme love of Rāma and Mādhava arose. (BhP 10.11.36)
[8] In that regard, Govardhana is introduced first as follows: "That which is known in the Purāṇa as Gokuleśvara belongs to Kṛṣṇa; Gokula is his abode."
And it is said that Govardhana is the very foundation of the cowherd settlement and the source of its prosperity; indeed, it is the repository of all treasures here.
And in this regard, there is this distinction:
she is known as the mental Gaṅgā of the three worlds, even piercing through Govardhana.
I think here, O Kṛṣṇa, that a stream born of affection enters into that interval.
Moreover,
in that place shines the pair of jasmine blossoms belonging to the couple Śrī Hari and Rādhā.

I believe that through their mutual intimacy, they perceive each other's fragrances; for from this, their love is made manifest, appearing as a pair of breaths accompanied by tremors and a state of swooning, moist with devotion, and taking the form of intense aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (JGc 1.1.9) [Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter]
[10] Moreover, this is the excellence of the Yamunā:
the daughter of the Sun does not merely bestow radiance upon those who have produced merit through bathing, but [bestows it] from the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu).
For even by a mere glance, she bears the supreme burden of the sweetness of the dark-hued Lord's splendor.
And therein they imagine:
by the power of the affection for the objects of the group that is as tender as a dog's.
Was it perhaps a spreading particle of perspiration from the dark-bodied Kṛṣṇa,
or was it the very affection of the group for the object of their love, Kṛṣṇa, that caused the Yamunā to flow with a course imbued by that same emotion?
[Vasantatilakā] [12] And her sandbanks manifest a great surge of love; for instance—
those which even today, by the mere sight of the wise, [bring joy].
Having contemplated the aesthetic flavor of the *rāsa* dance performed by Kṛṣṇa, they nourish it;
why then does the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) here laboriously gather her own sands with excellent elixirs and divine powders?
*Vasantatilakā* [13]:
But that Bhāṇḍīra tree agitates our minds;
for instance—how can the manifest love of Bhāṇḍīra for Hari be described?
When Hari had vanished, he who stood there with him likewise disappeared;
as if thinking, "Let Govardhana and the other mountains here become objects of affection for the world through their own portions, otherwise I would not be capable of creating this tenderness."
[In the Mandākrāntā meter] [14] Oh, behold the profound depth of love of this Vṛndāvana! For—
due to the guile of Agastya, here and there—
This forest of Hari has become motionless;
for the most part, the trembling of the leaves and the horripilation of the sprouts have ceased on all sides.
[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [15] As that son of the King of Vraja emerged from the multitude of people dwelling in Vraja, what was there that did not emerge, as if desiring to manifest itself?
And we perceive that this is indeed logical;
for the word *vraja* denotes a collection (*samūha*) consisting entirely of cows.

[16] And there is a verse here from the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam; beginning from that point, O King, Nanda’s Vraja became possessed of all prosperity, a playground for Lakṣmī due to its being the abode of Hari and His personal qualities.
Thus [it is said].

[17] According to the narrative of the *Padma Purāṇa*, regarding their manifestation, at the conclusion of the slaying of Dantavakra— an event that provides the wealth of no small happiness for every kalpa—
the entrance [of the Lord] will be proclaimed everywhere, even in a secluded and lovely place.

Therefore, everything arises from the extraordinary majesty of Vṛndāvana itself—which is free from the touch of the bodies and minds of worldly beings; which consists of the multitude of supreme glories celebrated by Varāha and others; and which is the treasury of the eternal pastimes of Tārāmā, Rāma, the cows, the cowherds, and Gopāla, whose unmixed descriptions are heard in the Padma, Skanda, and other Purāṇas.
For he who has transcended the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti-sthiti*),
the deposition of the summarized meaning of those various points is observed in the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa residing in the *Bṛhad-gautamīya*:
"This beautiful Vṛndāvana is indeed my own abode alone."
Here, my animals, birds, wild beasts, insects, humans, and gods—
who dwell in my abode— upon dying, go to my own realm.
The cowherd girls who dwell here in my abode are yoginīs; they are constantly devoted to my service.
My forest, which has the form of my body, extends for five yojanas;
here flows the Kālindī, known as the Suṣumṇā, which carries the supreme nectar.
Here the gods and all living beings exist in subtle form;
I am composed of all the gods, and I shall never abandon this forest.
"May there be for me manifestation and concealment here in age after age;
this beautiful, radiant reality is invisible to the physical eye.

[19] Indeed, regarding that particular manifestation of power (*vaibhava-viśeṣa*), which will be revealed in its proper place through the introduction of specific explanations by means of the essence of all things—

In accordance with the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Supreme Lord Himself— the abode of compassion— having come from His own realm to the cowherds from the ocean (the abode of Varuṇa), manifested His own opulence characterized by the excellence of Vaikuṇṭha by immersing and emerging from the bliss-bestowing Brahma-lake, thereby generating wonder among those people; thereafter, He protected them with His own self while being praised with Vedic hymns.

In this very Vṛndāvana, he displayed to others his common human pastimes in a manner distinct from those [other incarnations]; toward whom even today, the wise, by taking refuge, perceive those pastimes as if they were directly present even with their minds; and whom Mahendra, in the *Harivaṃśa*—in the section concerning the grandeur of Govinda’s consecration—demonstrated to be truly all-pervasive, appearing in a form identical to that of the son of the illustrious King of Vraja. Whom...

Furthermore, some describe that very Vṛndāvana—though situated near all [the other realms]—as being beyond the covering of material nature (prakṛti) and above the supreme ether (parama-viyad), according to their respective descriptions;
thus, by virtue of its form corresponding to the divine pastimes (līlā), they attain it as both finite and infinite, which are its various grounds (bhūmayaḥ).

This very same [Vṛndāvana], being non-different from the Residue (Śeṣa) and having the nature of the direct realization of Brahman, was described by the great sages as "expanded" (bṛṃhitam) in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* and other scriptures.

And therein, since Vṛndāvana consists of both manifest and unmanifest manifestations and possesses many various locations as heard in numerous scriptures, it is now specifically the particular glory of its unmanifest manifestation that is to be described. Since that glory has Gokula as its primary essence, this work, which is beneficial according to one’s own intention, is composed in accordance with the Brahma-saṃhitā.
However, his words are presented out of sequence for the sake of facilitating understanding, as follows:
"I worship that Śvetadvīpa, which they here call Goloka; those virtuous ones who know it are but a few, wandering sparsely upon the earth."
The beloveds of Śrī are beautiful, the Supreme Person is the beloved, the trees are wish-fulfilling kalpa-tarūs, the ground consists of clusters of cintāmaṇi jewels, and the water is nectar.
Where there is storytelling, song, dance, and even movement; where the flute, the dear friend, the light of supreme consciousness-bliss, and that which is to be tasted [the nectar] exist;
and where that great ocean of milk flows from the Surabhis.
"Indeed, not even a moment of time known as half a blink passes there.
Furthermore, beginning with "Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Lord," he says:
"The great abode called Gokula is a thousand-petaled lotus."
Its pericarp is that abode, born from His infinite portions;
its filaments are those portions, and its petals are even the Śrīs.
Surrounding that is the wonderful region called Śvetadvīpa, which is square;
it is the fourfold abode of the Fourfold Formed One, fashioned in four ways.
It is encompassed by the four aims of human life and the four causes,
and it is bound by ten spikes in the upward, downward, cardinal, and intermediate directions.
It was graced by the eight treasures as well as the eight supernatural powers,
and it was surrounded on all sides by the ten guardians of the directions in the form of Manu.
It was adorned on all sides by those wondrous spears and by the preeminent attendants, who were dark, fair, red, and white.
Moreover—
protecting the fragrant [goddesses] in palaces made of heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of kalpa-trees;
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person (Ādi-puruṣa), who is served with great reverence by hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs," and so forth—
thus it is said in the *Bṛhad-vāmana*.
There is the glorious Mount Govardhana, composed of precious gems,
and the Kālindī, the best of rivers, whose two banks are bound with jewels.
And so forth, as stated elsewhere.
Following this, first of all, the mere subject matter (*vastu-mātra*) of poetry— the foundation— is elucidated along with its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
like the canvas for a painting.

For instance— indeed, that world which, by its nature as Goloka, consists of cows and cowherds, and by its nature as Śvetadvīpa, possesses a self-nature awakened through a supreme purity untouched by anything else,
is considered to possess various forms of supremacy because its body consists of only a few objects of knowledge composed of such knowledge.
"Supreme Goloka" and "Supreme Śvetadvīpa"—
this alone is what has been rightly stated.
For it is there that the objects denoted by the word *gopī*— which signify the many who bestow the bliss of self-will— take refuge in Śrī.
Unlike other Vaikuṇṭhas, its singular designation is not limited in its meaning;

rather, it is established that those [names] have that as their referent because they teach the chanting of His mantra—which acts like a machine for extracting the essence of the meaning of His great speech—by virtue of His being the beloved of the cowherd girls (ballavī-vallabha).
Here, we do not rely solely on the conventional usage of that two-syllable word within its grammatical function (*vṛtti*).
Moreover, even regarding meditation (*dhyāna*):
however, the parrot’s statement, "This is not a limb of Śrī," reveals the conquest of ordinary *lakṣmī*;
whereas the speech of Viriñci, "a thousand Lakṣmīs," acknowledges the specific nature of this particular *lakṣmī*.
Since, in this context, it is accepted that the words *kuru* and *pāṇḍava* denote both the whole and the parts as appropriate to the occasion—
this being so,
even there, Rādhā is supreme.
What has been spoken in the Padma, Skanda, and other Purāṇas, as well as in the Vārāha, the Vimiśra, the Mātsya, and even in the Govinda-vṛndāvana-nāma-tantra— how could that be otherwise?
Lakṣmī is the most beautiful woman on all sides, and the gopīs are renowned as the most beautiful of Lakṣmīs;
yet if Rādhā is the most secret of all, what other woman could possibly be her equal? [Upagīti] [26] Thus, even among all those women of such a nature, there is but one who delights him.
For that very reason, he whose abode is Gokula and whose name is Govinda is the supreme among those great beings called "Lovers of Ramā," who individually delight each individual Ramā.
As for the fact that his status as a lover was manifested through *māyā* in the midst of them, [it was so].
That [world], indeed, being unreal, is subsequently sublated; this is established by the two terms "Śrī" and "Paramapuruṣa.
In this narrative, however, we shall establish it through the arrangement of specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this manner, the venerable Rāma, who is disciplined, is also indicated by extension (*atideśa*).
Furthermore, all these trees are indeed *kalpataru*s solely by virtue of the power of granting [desires] through mere thought (*saṅkalpa*),
and not because of any distinction between the venerable, the meritorious, the common, or the particular.
Moreover, among them, those that are *kalpataru*s by birth are defined precisely by their distinct characteristics.

[30] Furthermore, the ground—which consists of a palace as clear as a mirror, possessing the quality of being touchable like a mirror—is the source of splendor; or rather, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) that brings about the creation of showers of splendor.

[31] Let alone the subsequent greatness of the houses and other structures, which are accessible through a gradation of increasing beauty and are composed of great wish-fulfilling gems, for from them emerge those very excavations (*udbhida*).

They manifest his splendor within themselves; and there, even those species of mountains, deer, and birds that have not come within the range of sight or hearing, yet have become objects of his experience through their birth and form, bring wonder to the inhabitants of that place. (JGc 1.16) [Gīti]
[32] Furthermore, even water acts as nectar; how much more so, then, actual nectar? Moreover, even conversation is like song, acting as a draught for the ears.
How much more so their own singing?
Furthermore, even their walking adopts the preeminence of skill in dancing; as for dancing itself, it is truly beyond compare.
Furthermore, just as the flute quickly proclaims the blissful pastimes of the Enemy of Kaṃsa,
shines forth as His companion, and acts as His dear friend, no other person, however fortunate, can possibly do so.
Furthermore, Consciousness-Bhagavān alone, manifesting as specific individualities through the power of His manifestation which is non-different from His own essential nature,

assumes the role of the leader for each respective group of female companions— those who, like the inhabitants of Gokula whose worldly strength is derived from the power of the word "Gokula," engage in the exclusive pastimes of play by illuminating objects characterized as flowers and the like, and who thus fashion their speech through the tasting of those very objects such as flowers that have been illuminated.
The swarms of honey-sweet, low-pitched melodies (*kākalī*) sung there by those women— telling tales of supreme *apūrva*, of former loves, and so forth— moisten everything within that grove;
how much more so that very couple who have become united through the creation of many hardships?
And likewise, in the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, within the determination of the five principles (*pañca-tattva*), the principle of substance (*dravya-tattva*) residing in Vaikuṇṭha is described:
"Whatever substance consists of fragrance, form, and taste— such as flowers and the like—
it is material (*bhautika*) and exists here in the form of taste."
"And because of the absence of any portion to be discarded, that [essence] shall exist in the form of *rasa* (sap).
Know that whatever constitutes the skin, the seed, and the solid portion—all that is elemental (*bhautika*); for it is not composed of the primary elements (*bhūta*). And so forth.
Nevertheless,

O Lord, though You Yourself are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), You manifest such proliferation upon the earth in order to spread the mass of bliss for the multitude of people who have taken refuge in You.

Thus, according to the word of Brahmā, it is understood that the immersion (*yathāveśa*) of that person who has taken refuge and of Him [the Lord] occurs in the *līlā-sāra* (the essence of divine play), which manifests as a semblance of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-anukāra*), and not so in the eternal form (*nityākāra*). Furthermore, because of the absence of any elements to be rejected (*heyāṃśa*), that [divine form] consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasarūpa*). And His skin...
Know that whatever constitutes the seed, the portion to be abandoned, and the solid portion—all that is derivative (bhautika); for it is not composed of the primary elements (bhūta).
[36] Therefore, there would be an immersion (*āveśa*) of each respective [power] in the former, and an entry (*praveśa*) into the latter.
[37] Consequently, it should be discerned that by the power of His will, the power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*) manifests almost everything in the latter.
[38] Furthermore, the flute-playing skill (*khuralī*) of Murajit (Kṛṣṇa) on his muralī has milked the charming nectar of the cows of His own sweetness.
Spreading from the mountain-like udders of the Surabhis in every direction like rivers, she expands the ocean of milk which serves as her surrounding moat;
therein, because they are the wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenu), the flow of milk from those who yield it at will is brought to its ultimate abundance.
[39] Then those rivers, though possessing various flavors, are encountered by those possessed of knowledge.

[40] Furthermore, in that place, their fathers, brothers, friends, and all such groups remain in ages corresponding to childhood, middle age, youth, and fresh youth, and do not assume any other state.

[41] Furthermore, he whose own form manifests as the world named Gokula—residing in the center of that Goloka, which is indeed eternally and most clearly adorned with many thousands of petals—is a stainless great jewel-lotus; and he declares: "I am truly Vraja itself, the abode of cows and cowherds."
[42] Furthermore, this is indeed established by logic:
conventional usage (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga).
Just as the word "jalaja" does not denote merely that which is born in water, [but specifically a lotus].
But it is indeed the lotus;
for the mention of the term "conventional usage" (rūḍhi) clearly indicates that this is merely a matter of conventional designation.
The venerable Śukadeva also spoke with this in mind,
saying, "The Blessed One is the Lord of Gokula.
Here, the suffix *-varaṭ* indeed has the sense of characterizing a habitual disposition (*śīla*).
And that very Gokula has been traditionally taught as the forest-Vaikuntha.

Now, centered upon the pericarp of that Great Lord— who possesses the character and pastimes of the son of the illustrious King of Vraja— there shines forth with intense brilliance a great jewel-made abode, described as a treasury of manifold-colored splendors.
That which, having arisen from its own infinite parts, clearly manifests in infinite ways;

in which the cowherds dwell nearby with compassion, their kin, along with their wives and children, surrounding it on all sides at the same time, amidst the spreading filaments of its stalks. // JGc 1.1.17 // [Gīti]

[45] That too is consistent with the logic of the cowherd community (*gokulatābala*). For instance, parts, portions, and inheritances (*aṃśa*, *bhāga*, *dāya*)—by virtue of their connection to what is beneficial for them—are possessed by those who have an inheritance (*dāyavat*).
Indeed, those who are born from a caste (*jāti*) are its portions (*bhāga*), and thus they possess that inheritance (*dāyavat*). [In the *gīti* meter.]
Alternatively, it may be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those who have a portion (*aṃśa*) in that [Supreme Being].
In the case of their application, it is appropriate that rice-like love for Him rests upon them. [Udgīti] [46] Thus, Śrī Śuka has stated that they indeed possess that very nature.
"Thus, having slain Kakudmin while being praised by his own kinsmen, He—
along with His attendants and a festival for the eyes of the cowherd women— entered the cow-pen.

In their preeminent residence, the two— Rāma and Ajita— honored upon a jeweled throne, took food and other offerings from the hands of their brides and were served by their two mothers;
while eating, they were surrounded by friends with playful jests, causing those friends to laugh aloud.
And by means of that festival, the couple brought joy to all their attendants.
[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] [3] After the meal, while the illustrious Śrīmatī— accompanied by her mother— was looking on with tears and listening with a smile,
the noble prince of Vraja engaged in pleasant conversation with various topics with his elder brother and his friends.
At the command of the King of Vraja, he entered [the assembly], saying: "My child, the members of the assembly, having been honored in the hall, shine with splendor;
and those two sons of the charioteer remain there, upholding their own tradition."
And then,
having bowed to his mother who gave her permission, he quickly went with Anurāma to the assembly of courtiers.
Then that pair, endowed with light, acted like a friend to the night-lotuses, causing the beds of lilies to bloom.

[4] Therein, the inner [structure] consists of a series of rooms attached to rows of pillars surrounding the entrance to the assembly hall; this fifth [section], situated in the eastern direction, possesses a form suitable for supporting a thousand worlds. It is divided into two parts by a wall constructed with a network of fine lattice apertures both internally and externally, and its length is arranged such that it is bisected by a low-lying path running crosswise through the middle, wherein four paved floors are obtained both inside and out.
Seated appropriately upon clusters of jeweled thrones that encircled the two outer paved courtyards, they shone with extraordinary joy; therein,
regarding the radiant row of seats constructed on the northern pavement and facing southward—

The illustrious King of Vraja was resplendent; on his left side, the illustrious Crown Prince of Vraja, having established a joyful assembly, took his place by a row of treasure-chests fixed against that bank facing eastward, while on the right side,
accompanied by a multitude of the best of earthly gods, he sat most comfortably, having reached a pleasant line of structures built close to the wall along that bank facing eastward.
The family priest shone resplendently there;
and some heroic Ābhīras, positioned upon the western pavement, were also shining.
Furthermore, the central portion between those two pavements rose higher than the courtyard.
He himself, however, shone brilliantly, being well-visible from the paved floors due to his vastness and because he was not too low;
facing the glorious sovereign of Goloka, those two sons of Sūta stood between the two paved floors with their hands joined at the fingertips, rising together with their companion.

And on both sides, to the left and right, all those residing in Vraja, including the charioteers and others, sat upon a vast courtyard distinguished by the presence of shimmering Arhat-thrones; while the other refined ones sat elsewhere.
Thus it being arranged, he was seated upon a great lion-throne made of jewels, which rose higher than everything else.
Desired by the virtuous, his hands adorned with excellent scattered flowers and other offerings, he entered the midst of his brothers;
repeatedly casting a gaze like a shower of nectar upon the face of Kṛṣṇa with longing,
the glorious King of Goloka was seen shining in the assembly by the subjects.
Śrī Rāmadāsa and others, whose lower garments meet upon their seats of white cushions, slightly emerge from behind the crescent-shaped pillows;
they delight the assembly with their smiling glances.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is perceived here even now, as if visibly present before our eyes.

And therein, his complexion and so forth are described in this way: "When the light was dark, it suddenly assumed a dark state; likewise, when it was red, it attained redness; when the radiance was yellow, it took on a yellow luster; and in its various forms, it reached a state of multicolored diversity."
At that very moment, the path of the eyes of the people, captivated by the luster of Hari’s major and minor limbs,
seemed to mock the various forms and movements of the actors through the manifestation of His smile.
Moreover:
This is the moon; this is the dark first rain-cloud; by its splendors it is the lamp of the universe;
those lightnings shine here, yet they instantly abandon their own existence. But these [others]...
"Are the stars here dissolved? "No, O fool! It is the sky, it is the assembly hall!
Thus, out of mutual amusement, there arose among the poets there a constant debate.
[8] Right there, upon the poetry of another certain person, a swarm of bees hovered over his surface, which was like a smiling blue lotus pond.
Following that, O friend, a flood of light from the son of the Sun shines forth; what is this new assembly?
[9] Then, joined with Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma in the place of the Self, the renowned Śrīdāmā,

having informed the illustrious King of Vraja, immediately entered the center of the city; being successful, he clearly ascended higher and higher, exceeding even by a fraction the boundary of the courtyard that was somewhat elevated above the outer pavement, along with the Queen of Vraja and her attendants.

Having brought together those whose bodies were joined, who were worthy of being seen merely through close proximity, and who were adorned by their rows; having arranged them in a dense network of many interlacing lattices;

and having introduced the chamberlain along with his attendants; he then enacted the gathering of those women within the assembly hall by means of a mere glance, and sat down once more not far from the two of them.
[10] There, in the company of illustrious friends, even Madhumangala entered as if upon a stage, assuming, through various conversations, the role of bestowing joy by means of humorous jests.
[11] There, upon a magnificent jewel-studded throne belonging to the illustrious Queen of Vraja, amidst the principal guests—
With the regions before her served by her sons and their young brides,
Kṛṣṇa’s mother shone as she drank in from the window the moon-like splendor of her sons’ faces, thirsting for the account of their virtuous deeds.
[12] Then the king sweetly commanded Vraja: “O Madhukaṇṭha and Snigdhakaṇṭha!
We are longing;
therefore, let something be lifted up.”
[13] With palms joined in reverence, the two said: “O Lord, relying upon what course of action should we proceed?
[14] Vrajarāja replied: “Let them be known as omniscient; let them amaze us by means of their own narratives.”
The two of them said: “As you are the foremost of those who guide the disciplined, nevertheless, let one of us two, who are like young fawns, be commanded so that the other may become a listener.”
[16] Vrajarāja said: “Let each one attain that respective form every single day, with an interval of one day between them;
however, that which has already commenced is ordained to remain as it was, superior indeed.
[17] Thereupon, Madhukaṇṭha, his longing held fast, immediately gladdened everyone by reciting the *nāndī* with palms joined in reverence, as follows:
To the illustrious Lord Brahmā himself who triumphs, to the great celestial sage Vyāsa who was born from him, to Parīkṣit, and also to Ugraśravas and Śaunaka—
those who are devoted to the renown of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and who deliver the entire world.
To proclaim the greatness of the illustrious Goṣṭha, we pay homage to those who are full of longing.
And then— afterwards, taking up a small pair of cymbals, two experts in the *maḍḍuka* drums sang at their sides.
He whose left ear is at the tip of the other [hand],
this speaker has indeed gratified everything loudly.

[18] When this manner had been established, Madhukaṇṭha, having attained the essence of the matter, began the narrative, singing with longing, dancing, and expressing various emotional states (*bhāva*). Now begins the narrative:
[19] Thus—now, the ornament of the Vṛṣṇi lineage, whose praises are celebrated in all the Vedas and Purāṇas, the supreme abode of virtues named Śrī Devamīḍha, resided in Madhurā.
And that crest-jewel among noble men had two wives:
the first was of the second caste, while the second was of the third caste.
And from those two, in due order, two sons were born as was fitting; the first was Śūra, [and the second] Parjanya.
Among them, from Śūra arose the illustrious Vasudeva and others.
But the glorious Parjanya, according to the principle that "one who resembles his mother is of mixed caste," entered the status of a Vaiśya and brought the cattle under his own control.
He took up residence in the very forest of Bṛhadvana; and from his childhood, he honored those who came to see him as Brahmins,
fulfilling their desires and raining down gifts upon them.
He was devoted to the Vaiṣṇava Veda, he practiced according to the Veda as long as he lived, and he worshipped Hari throughout his entire life.
And his mother’s lineage, being praised as the crest-jewel of the people who pervade all directions, was most worthy of commendation;
for it attained distinction because it was proclaimed by the virtuous as a particular branch of the Ābhīras.
And likewise Manu says:
"From a Brāhmaṇa, on a maiden of the Ugra caste, one named Āvṛta is born;
on a maiden of the Ambaṣṭha caste, an Ābhīra; but on an Āyogava maiden, a Dhigvaṇa" (Manu 10.15).
Elsewhere it is said: "An Ambaṣṭha is one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a daughter of the Vaiśyas.
Therefore, it is well known that even Brahmā, while performing a sacrifice, accepted a Gopī—a girl belonging to the lineage of Ābhīras (cowherds)—as his wife;
this very Gopa lineage will be integrated into the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This has been made clear in the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa itself.
Therefore, this lineage of the Mahābhīra twice-born, who are included among the Vaiśyas, is indeed most praiseworthy.
[21] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha thought within himself: "Even so, alas, some might even cast doubt upon their status as twice-born."
Indeed, in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, in the speech of the illustrious King of Vraja to Garga— beginning with the words, "O Kuru, perform the purificatory rites for the twice-born" (10.8.10),
and continuing from "A Vaiśya should live by his livelihood"— it is stated that agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and moneylending are called the fourth [means of livelihood].
In Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s words to the King of Vraja: "There, the livelihood is fourfold; we are constantly engaged in the occupation of cowherds" (BhP 10.24.20–21);
and in Śrī Śuka’s description of the cowherd settlement: "Fire, the sun, guests, cows, and brāhmaṇas... (BhP 10.46.12).

"But by way of contrast, even though Vidura acted as a King of Dharma (*dharma-rāja*) and was heard of for his conduct that was otherwise [than a Śūdra's] due to being born from the womb of a Śūdra woman, they will consider him superior.
[22] Then he spoke clearly: "And what happened after that?
[23] Madhukaṇṭha said: "And that illustrious Parjanya, by means of his own sovereignty—acquired through the excellence of his benevolence—transcended the commonality shared with other Vaiśyas."
And this was not surprising,

for he attained a likeness to the rain-cloud through his protection of the region inhabited by him, his honorability, his generosity, and his preeminence gained by inundating all the people with the abundance of his milk;
indeed, he was Prahlāda in fame.
Dhruva is in a promise, Pṛthu in greatness,
and Bhīṣma in a wicked-hearted person.
Śaṅkara was his friend, Svayambhū was his dignity, and Hari was his splendor.

And those cowherds, born of a great maternal lineage, who possessed mastery even over the calculation of their multitude of virtues by all—even when counted by the thousands—remained inexhaustible; they, along with their teachers, came to take refuge with him of their own accord.
And in groups, those leaders of the illustrious assembly of the Yadus, headed by Ugrasena, [honored] him who was indeed preeminent in the weight of all virtues.
Beholding him as the foremost of the assembly, they honored him with a tilaka that was the very ornament of his sovereignty over the entire world of cowherds;
he whose beloved wife was the most excellent among the excellent, preeminent in all virtues;
and he whose five illustrious sons, beginning with Upananda, brought joy to the whole world.
[24] And thus the panegyrists bring out the poetic quality of his verse: "But this one is a rain-cloud of water, whereas he is a rain-cloud of happiness;
for he constantly refreshes the people with his creations, such as the *Upananda* and other works."
Parjanya was perceived on earth as the visible mark of those whose livelihood is agriculture;
that he attained such gross visibility is not at all surprising.
And there is this analogy:
Upānanda and these others are indeed the five forms of the Father, just as "the dear" and so forth are [the forms] of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) in the Vedāntas. (1.3.14)
And they speculate:
"By giving his sons the names Upananda, Abhinanda, Nanda, Sannanda, and Nandana, their father has severely punished the very meaning of the word 'Nanda'."
[25] Thus, while all his prosperities were present, the prosperity of his sons attained the highest degree of delight,
like the excellence of garments among the excellences of finery;
even therein, the prosperity of the middle son was like the central excellence in a continuous row of sovereign powers.
[26] Here, some liken him to Arjuna;
we, however, do not consider that son of Pāṇḍu—a mere child in comparison to the glorious Parjanya-nandana, who stands in the midst of all gladdening beings—to be a fitting analogy for him.
Moreover, among those most noble brothers, he does not merely exist as their middle one by birth alone, but also by his very position in the center.
Moreover, by being the locus of the perfection of affection, it was not only for them but for everyone;
whereby, even more than for his parents, there arose in him an ever-increasing abundance of love, which served to perpetually increase the happiness of his brothers and was never a cause for rivalry.
Yet, such an abundance of excellent qualities has not manifested in him;

rather, there is a manifestation of a particular devotion toward the Blessed One within himself. For as the divine Goddess of Speech in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* declares: "In whomsoever there is unalloyed devotion to the Blessed One, in him all divine virtues reside. [27]

[28] Having heard this from Madhukaṇṭha, the illustrious Upananda said softly to the illustrious Abhinanda: "Does he possess the knowledge of others' hearts merely by recounting a story he has learned? [29] Then Abhinanda, having understood that, spoke to Madhukaṇṭha with wonder: "And then? What happened next?
[30] Madhukaṇṭha said: "That being so, a most fortunate maiden was given to him by a certain man named Sumukha, acting on behalf of the cowherds."
Indeed, she bestows fame upon her own people who have been won over by her virtues— how much more so upon those who hear it,
how much more so upon those who see it, and how much more so upon those who are devoted!
And so, by their union as husband and wife at that very moment, happiness and prosperity arose for everyone, let alone for their mother, father, and others.
Thus, having gladdened all living beings and being free from resentment, the rain-cloud itself became auspicious in every respect.

Having experienced even greater happiness and regarding himself as a guest among householders, he considered his own bodily maintenance to be fulfilled solely by the worship of the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda; thus, desiring to bestow the status of the ornament of his entire lineage upon the most venerable of the venerable,
he wished to offer him the ceremonial mark (*tilaka*).
Having constructed an assembly hall that shone with the presence of Vasudeva and other lords of men, as well as Garga and other gods on earth, he bestowed it upon them.

Furthermore, having accepted his father’s command and fulfilled his duty, he summoned those of great majesty—including Vasudeva and others—to that very assembly hall; and placing his own middle younger brother, who was naturally fond of his lap, upon his lap, he adorned him with that *tilaka*.
He honored him with the sovereignty over Gokula.

Then, while his younger brother shrank back and all the people there were filled with wonder, and while his father’s eyes shone with joy, he said: "I have not acted without reflection in this matter, for everyone is subject to the succession of affections."
And that [excellence] belongs to virtue,
and that [virtue] belongs to total consistency;
and that [consistency] exists here in one way or another, but not in one such as me.
Indeed, she alone deserves the freedom of one who has mastery over all. Moreover, even the Inner Controller of all makes him his own.
Behold: while this assembly is shining forth, the multitude of eyes of everyone, like bees, hover playfully about his lotus-like face alone.
Thus, from the very beginning, conformity to that [name] is conceived here;
let this too be conceived by means of my name alone:
"Therefore, he is our king."
Then, along with a rain of flowers, a clear sound of "Well done! Well done!
arose from the members of the assembly here, who gazed upward toward heaven with wide-open eyes.
Just as there was the auspicious sound of "Victory! Victory! resounding everywhere.
[35] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "O illustrious Madhukaṇṭha, who has caused longing for the world through your sweet voice!
Among the three sons of the illustrious Upanandanandana, who is this one called 'Madhyama'?
Or what is his true nature? Let it be told with examples."
[36] Madhukaṇṭha said: "First, let this faultless *pravahlikā* verse, appropriate for the delight of your mind, be completed.
[37] Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "Certainly.
[38] Madhukaṇṭha said:
"He has brought my son away and, by making him his own son, enjoys prosperity;
he knows this for himself, yet he does not [share] friendship with him."
"Who is this that pierces [me] and speaks thus in my mouth? he said.
[39] With a tender voice and out of longing, he spoke quickly and joyfully: "It is indeed Nanda!
[40] Madhukaṇṭha said: "This has surely been known by you;
therefore, let this be heard."

This very King of Vraja is one who always desires for his own worship and happiness a greater measure of joy through even a small virtue of his own, yet through that same virtue, however great it may be, he always seeks the welfare of others;
such is He who, in order to delight the son of Śūra, [manifested Himself].
Unable to endure even the slightest loss of that [friendship], he did not perceive even the smallest difference between them.

[41] Then, having obtained this nectar-moon of Madhukanda’s hymn, the assembly of internal and external scholars— like a jewel-mine with its surging waves of limbs— scattered a heart-captivating string of jewels upon it, or rather bestowed a garland of hearts; indeed, they themselves could not discern the difference between the two.
[42] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "And then? What happened next?

[43] Madhukaṇṭha replied: "Thereafter, that illustrious and blessed Parjanya, entering Vṛndāvana to worship the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda, briefly instructed his sons—who were inquiring about the essence of all the scriptures—as follows:"

"What is the root of fear? That which is unseen. What is the refuge? A devotee of Śrī Hari. What is to be prayed for? Devotion to Him. What is happiness? Supreme love for Him. (JGc 1.3.19) Thus, when that noble one had gone to Vṛndāvana together with his wife, the illustrious Upananda, in accordance with his own name, spoke without restraint in the assembly of the great lord of the glorious Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
He remained like Bhīṣma in the assembly hall of Vicitravīrya; even he,
under the pretext of counsel, specifically following his command alone, protected the entire multitude of subjects as a good king at all times.

And therein, his conduct and practice became a marvel, as follows: he never transgressed his father's command in any matter, whether it concerned dharma and so forth, or even matters of worldly profit.
Prosperity was never again subject to him, by which he might have attained further growth by force.
[46] Thus, while the entire multitude of Vraja had attained prosperity, growth, and success under a righteous king, a certain longing, appearing like the Kali age itself, gradually began to blossom:
that no offspring was born to that king, who was dear as life to all his own kinsmen. And as time passed, due to the failure of hope, it brought extreme distress upon every person.
But they [the elder brothers and others] did so even more intensely;
as for the illustrious Lord of Vraja and his consort, however, they had already been moistening the desire for progeny from the outset,
and they did so especially thereafter.

Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "How is it that they did not have their sons perform the *putreṣṭi* and other such rites? Or how did doubt arise even for those two, who were so wise? Furthermore, how could there be any hope for them, who were devoted solely to the Supreme Lord?"
"But how was it especially so in the north?
[48] Madhukaṇṭha said: "Even though that was performed, it did not attain stability.
[49] Snigdhakaṇṭha asked: "How was that?"
Or how else could it be otherwise?
[50] Madhukaṇṭha said: "For indeed, this conversation took place in private between that very couple, even though they possessed every possible excellence."
As the illustrious husband said: "O mistress of the household, why does this world, overcome by grief, prepare canopies and the like for my funeral?
For at the very moment of my forming this resolve, my mind was intent upon a son of such universal variety."
But how can that which is the supreme and unprecedented itself become an object of the unprecedented?
Consequently, the activity of the mind shrinks back from attempting to describe it further in words.
For what indeed could be sweeter than the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to compassion for me and whose very essence is the fruit of the complete study of the Vedas?
Like a sky-flower compared to a *parijāta* blossom, [51] then Snigdhakaṇṭha reflected: "It is not improper that this [song] should be even sweeter than that;
for with reference to this, there is a verse from the *Śrī-Bhāgavata*: [Verse follows]"
That which was assumed by Him, who displayed the power of His own yoga-māyā for the sake of His pastimes as a mortal,
was intended to cause wonder at the excellence of His own opulence.
"The supreme state, whose limbs are adorned by ornaments" (BhP 3.2.12). Then he asked clearly, "What happened next? What happened next?
Madhukaṇṭha said: "Then his illustrious wife spoke: 'Please tell me, what kind of form did that have?'"
He said:
"That dark child with tremulous, beautiful, long eyes, clearly seen by me playing upon the surface of your lap where your milk-exuding breasts rest— "
Is this a dream, or is it waking reality? This cannot be determined.
Tell me truly, O fellow seeker of dharma: does that very same [world] manifest within you as well?
[55] He said: "O Illustrious One, this very mental state of mine also exists, surpassing the range of the intellect;
it is only out of sheer shame that I have never before revealed it to you."
"Therefore, exerting ourselves in the investigation of the scriptures on renunciation, let us both restrain the mind itself from these impossible desires.

He said: "Even though this very point is clearly understood by me from time to time, nevertheless, my mental state turns toward the thought that the venerable Lord Nārāyaṇa alone—the great companion who possesses infinite mastery over the entire universe—is our refuge; for he has shown us this which was previously unseen and unheard."
He acts as if he were doing so;
he should perform even that which has been done before.
He said, "O King!"
"We perceive that for this deity, only one who is suitable for service is fit here.
He replied, "Certainly;
but what is she like?"
[59] She spoke, appearing in the form of the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata).
[60] He said with joy: "You speak what is appropriate;
even for me, this very same longing had sprouted and was throbbing within."
"Therefore, let this vow be undertaken starting from today.
As they were thus conversing, the sound of the celestial drums arising completely surpassed everything else.

Then, his inner heart loosened by that story which spread the activity of his own mind regarding her conduct, the beloved of the earth of Vraja bestowed his own beautiful array of ornaments upon the charioteer’s son.
The illustrious wife of the Lord of Vraja caused a necklace with a central gem of great sapphire to be fashioned.
Then, with longing, Snigdhakaṇṭha asked: "What then happened?
Madhukaṇṭha replied: "When that vow was completed at the end of the year and their thirst for Him had increased, the God of gods simultaneously appeared to them both in a dream."
And he said: "Aho!
How is it that you, being so deeply attached and devoted to me, have become disillusioned and distressed?
That youth, as delicate as an *atasī* flower, who has constantly appeared before you both in his state of childhood—"

He, however, has always followed only you two, in order to promote his own devotion at every kalpa; for the sake of directly perceiving that fruit— which is unattainable even by Brahmā and others— by means of a portion of the digit of the form of the earth (Dharā) established by me in heaven, he himself indeed takes birth on earth after you two, and before long, this beautiful [birth] will become most radiant.
The success of you two was turned back.
Thus, when the Blessed One—who had been made to hear, who had spoken, and who had departed for the supreme benefit—had vanished, they became wide awake as if having reached an ocean of nectar;
conversing with one another about that very same thing and spreading a multitude of supreme wonders, they carried themselves with great joy.
[66] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha reflected to himself: "Thus, the answers to my questions have indeed arisen;

and that they belong to these two is precisely what was rightly said by the Blessed Lord: 'Previously, this son of yours was born somewhere as the son of Vasudeva' (10.8.14)—even as the Sage speaks, whose flow of speech never deviates from the truth."
This appears to be the general intention of Śrī Garga:
that the relationship with the Blessed Lord is indeed based solely on pure love, as indicated by such statements as, "I am to be attained by devotion alone" (BhP 11.14.21).

Therefore, for a particular instance of that relationship, a particular instance of that very love is the cause, as indicated by such statements as, "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).
Then, in him who is truly a calf, that very love called *vātsalya* (parental affection) brings about his death.
In this regard, through the contemplation of his divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), Vasudeva attained both agitation and composure regarding that *vātsalya*;
however, in the illustrious King of Vraja, that *vātsalya* is renowned as being eternally awakened and purely pure.
The sages consider the mind alone to be the cause for parents bearing a child, as seen in such passages as:
"By a portion of his own self, the mind entered the womb of Ānakadundubhi" (BhP 10.2.26); and also in:
"She bore him who is the soul of all and identical with the Self, who brings bliss beyond the mind, just as the final goal [of sound] does" (BhP 10.2.18).

Even for the illustrious King of Vraja and his queen, the mental perception of Him is possible only through the natural inclination of devotion, which is established by the impossibility of any other explanation. And since that is so, it is especially now—following His supreme state—that such an arising occurs when devotion has been rendered with complete attachment.
Therefore, He is indeed your own son, who has appeared for some specific purpose or occasion involving Vasudeva.
[69] Then Prakaṭa said: "And then? And then?

[70] Madhukaṇṭha said: "Thus, when that longing had reached its highest intensity due to supreme distress, once all the inhabitants of Vraja, including their children, gathered together in an assembly;
and having assembled, they praised that very same longing with great fervor."
[71] At that time, a certain female ascetic arrived there together with a *snātaka*.

Observing her to possess the marks of great spiritual power, they all rose and, having performed the rites of hospitality without fail, made this inquiry: "Who are you? Are you the personified *yogamāyā* of the Blessed One, or perhaps the fresh incarnation of the illustrious Nārada?"
And she said with a laugh: "I am Paurṇamāsī by name, as well as Kātyāyanī, Kumāraśramaṇā, Pārikāṅkṣiṇī, and Ikṣaṇikā.
And this one named Madhumaṅgala is a *snātaka* of the nature of Śrī Nārada.
We two have always mastered these sciences through our particular expertise, even though we are of the same age."

[73] They said: "How is it that such great compassion has been shown toward us, who are so wretched? [74] She replied: "Having considered some degree of prosperity in you. [75] They all asked: "What is that?"
[76] He said: "That very son who shall bring joy to the world will indeed be born from the life-root of you all, the illustrious Nanda.
[77] All of them, their hair standing on end and filled with tears, said: "This great forest of ours shall become a great sacred site (tīrtha).
Therefore, since rest has been granted to us by Kṛṣṇa, we shall clearly construct a hut for you near him."
[78] He said: "This is a hearsay that, though appearing in the guise of sacred revelation, is not even new, nor is it free from error;
for although it was intended to say 'of Kṛṣṇā,' it indicates 'of Kṛṣṇa.
For he shall indeed be named Kṛṣṇa."
When he, possessed of great majesty, is born, the earth shall become free from demons;
yet his virtues shall always remain fresh,
for while there is excellence in the continuous flow of knowledge and the like, there is a lack of such qualities in that which is unrelated to him.

"Having possessions when there is abundance of sense objects, but being without possessions when devoted to Him"—this and other such statements, though appearing contradictory, will be accepted by all.
Therefore, our insistence on remaining here has resulted in a favor for you.

[79] Then, all of them, bowing with joy and finding that [hermitage] which surpassed the beauty of the Indīvara lotus and eclipsed the Kālindī river, filled the leaf-hut and caused her to dwell there.

On that very day, during the evening when all faults had departed, Rohiṇī— the benefactress of Vraja and rider of the mare Baḍavā— arrived secretly, sent by Vasudeva, who was consumed by intense anger toward Kaṃsa, whose heart was withered, and who had uttered lamentations. Upon the arrival of that most devoted wife, the entire assembly of the kings and rulers of Vraja rejoiced together with a multitude of birds and other creatures filled with auspicious omens.
And there, O Ānanda, Śrī Yaśodā and Rohiṇī—like the Yamunā and Gaṅgā—being closely united, brought forth a multitude of happiness for one another and for others.

And the wife of the King of Vraja, having taken hold of her seniority and considering that her pregnancy had lasted three months, attained a state of joy through the very realization of their non-difference.

[82] Then, on the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, during a night filled with the expansion of every pleasure, she, while being attended by the King of Vraja, feeling overcome by drowsiness, beheld a certain beautiful vision gathered like a dream. [83] It was as if that very boy, having concealed himself from all sides by means of a certain divine maiden who acted as his veil, entered her own heart from the heart of the King of Vraja, appearing as if visible.
"Remaining thus," he said; and consequently, he occupied the center of the heart-lotus,
while she occupied the center of the belly.

And Vrajarāja, having for a long time experienced that indescribable state of being possessed by their constant entry into his own heart, cast off his distress and experienced it in that very same way.

[84] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha reflected within himself: "This is indeed true; for this very reason, those endowed with the virtues of noble speech have repeatedly considered these two to be his own sons. And through careful deliberation, I myself previously determined and acted accordingly."
And he asked: "What happened after that?

Madhukaṇṭha replied: "From that time forward, having perceived the signs of pregnancy, she became the bringer of happiness to the noble ladies of Gokula, who were both present and those yet to be born.
For instance—"
When Yaśodā’s pregnancy had advanced, her face became pale, the tips of her breasts grew full, and her belly rose high and prominent, as if it had become an informer [of the secret within].
And just as Kṛṣṇa, whose self vibrates within the Queen of Vraja, vibrates in the world as well—
just like a lamp that shines both inside and outside a crystal jar, he is similar to that.
But then,
though she had conquered her tongue, possessed sweetness and fortitude, and was skilled in gravity and other virtues,
the wife of the King of Vraja nevertheless displayed this and that longing.

She was like the full moon because she shone with dense, radiant whiteness;
like a lioness toward her cub because she displayed a sequence of valorous strides; and like a fresh lotus plant toward its white lotus because she bore a stream of stainless fragrance.
Because he is the auspiciousness of the entire assembly of hearers, he is like a mass of fame consisting of irreproachable knowledge;
moreover,
his face is like the moon and his eyes are like a row of lightning flashes.
Rohiṇī gave birth to him whose hair was like that of a nine-year-old, whose body was like an autumnal cloud, and who possessed the splendor of the sun;
for he was indeed a divine child, and thus it was fitting.
And he is this one of dark stature yet white-statured, together with his younger brother;
the slayer of the Danujas, the protector of Dhenuka and the crusher of Dhenuka; possessed of long arms, the destroyer of Pralamba.

His birth rites and other ceremonies were performed by those skilled in the vital points (*marmaga*), using names ending in "Śarman" for his protection; this was done sufficiently because they were dependent on the counsel of Ānaka and Dundubhi.

And as they describe even now:

In the yoga named Harṣaṇa, under the pure lunar mansion of Purṇa, the supreme Lord Śrī-Vidhu himself arose at dawn for the joy of Nanda and his wife, dispelling the darkness.
And so it was:
at that time, on the night of Kṛṣṇa’s birth-star, those gods of the beginning of the Yuga quickly attended upon him, each bringing his own gift for his respective station.
For just as meditation did not flourish without truth, nor sacrifice without the Tretā age,
nor the worship of Hari without the Dvāpara age, so too the Name does not flourish without the Kali age.
Without honey there is no *saptalā* and the like; without heat there is no ripening of mangoes; without the beauty of autumnal rain there is no rice; and for her, there is nothing beyond that.
Without the cold season, there is no blooming of the lotus in the month of Māgha;
without the science of astronomy, the positions of the planets do not bestow auspiciousness.
Without the power of a guru, there is no manifestation of Hari anywhere;
yet he was born by Yaśodā even without the conventional process of birth.
[91] This will be clarified further ahead. Moreover:
In the midst of it is the sky, the essence of the ocean of stars;
at its edge is the realm above the oceans, a kinsman to the thundering clouds.
Thus, on that lunar day, the autumnal splendor— its thirst for the rainy season having been quenched— received the guest-hospitality due to her in a truly fitting manner.
Furthermore:

when the southern quarter was such that the *mādhavī* jasmines blossomed along with the *jāti* flowers, the *ketakī* lilies together with the *ketaka* trees, and the water-lilies (*kumud*) alongside the lotuses (*ambuja*).
Then even that is not a marvel, for it is fully understood by the masters,
since He, the treasury of all wonders, has entered into the course of birth and conduct.
For thus it is said: "To those who have cultivated this and will behold it in the future, his face appears like that of a lord of blooming, smiling, and dark lotuses;
his pair of eyes is like the inner petals of a white water-lily variegated with fine black bees."
Her nose belongs to the company of blue clouds, black sesame seeds, and tilaka flowers;
her lower lip to the assembly of vermilion, Mount Abja, hibiscus, and bimba fruits;
and her pair of ears to the young shoots of the dark creepers growing from the soil of collyrium.
His pair of arms, lovely with the tips of his hands, surpasses the branches of fresh *tāla* trees with their new sprouts;

A lotus with her two eyes,

a tortoise from the backs of his feet,

what need is there for much? Even Mukunda himself is his own. Thus, it is not impossible that at this very moment, there should be a simultaneous gathering here of those various occasions for their manifestation, as well as of those treasures whose presence is so difficult to attain.
