[96] Now, Snigdhakaṇṭha has explained this with authoritative evidence: "She is the invisible younger sister of Viṣṇu, possessing eight great arms equipped with weapons" (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.4.9), and because of the designation of "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) through terms such as "son" (*ātmaja*) in passages like "But Nanda, his son born, was filled with joy, the high-minded one" (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.5.1), she is described as having both a localized form (*sadeśa-rūpa*) and her true nature;
however, we ask about this very point explicitly and analytically so that the doubt of everyone may be pacified.
[97] He spoke clearly as well: "O Noble One, if that is so, then how is he identified as the son of Vasudeva and Devakī?

[98] When such words were spoken by Snigdhakaṇṭha, Madhukaṇṭha, his voice somewhat faltering, thought to himself: "The illustrious celestial sage has instructed us with great joy—if ever, in the illustrious..."

O you who possess great love, when the opportunity for conversation arises between you two, who have established yourselves in Vraja, then the all-pervading sovereignty of Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva must be concealed; therefore, we shall converse by relying solely on the doctrine of Garga, which is well-known among the circle of sages.
Since that doctrine has already been heard by these people, it will not result in any cause for wonder.
[99] And he spoke openly: "In this matter, my transgression in revealing this secret of the son of the illustrious King of Vraja must certainly be forgiven by him himself.
For in him resides a singular perfection that has attained excellence in every respect:

namely, that although his heart is always filled with affection for all, he remains ever-present within the hearts of those people who are anointed with love, reflected there even when he is out of sight through the seal of their own internal disposition."
He becomes sealed;
and his manifestation in his own essential form occurs entirely through the power of the fulfillment of the surging flow consisting of affection,
and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the seed for the manifestation as a son is precisely the affection consisting of the state of being a father, and not anything else as it is for others.

And once the manifestation as a son has occurred in some instance, the cause for the manifestation in such and such a manner through that particular state is simply the emergence of an accumulation produced by the affection consisting of those various relationships.
[100] This being the case, for the King of Vraja and others, who possess a variety of pure parental and other states fully awakened in every respect—

He shines eternally as the son and so forth of those very people of Vraja— from the hired laborers down to the residents— who appear at the beginning of every pair of *parārdhas* and every *kalpa*; for them, whose livelihood is growth, He manifests the expansion of the overflowing of their accumulated love, and relinquishing the resolve to repay it— out of the perception that its increase is immeasurable— He ever remains manifest.
Indeed, others there do not obtain even a sesame seed’s worth of space or time;
this very point was stated by Brahmā in the passage beginning with, "O Lord, are you the protector of these inhabitants of Ghoṣa? (BhP 10.14.35), and so forth.
And this same point was commanded by the divine Śrī Nārāyaṇa in the passage beginning with, "That youth who is as delicate as the *atasī* flower... and so forth. And therefore—
"Therefore, this son of Nanda is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities;
protect him with focused attention through your fortune, fame, and majesty.
Following these words of Garga, we reflect upon this: that he possesses all the wealth necessary for the sake of his own son alone, who is his very form.
The internal potency of that Great Blessed One— who is honored by the illustrious Lord of Vraja and whose power, known as Yogamāyā, which accomplishes the impossible, is described in the scriptures—
was indeed bestowed by Him upon Your son, Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone, where it found its ultimate fulfillment.
And although, because his mind is fixed on affection for his own kinsmen, he does not generally pay attention to this son of his here,
nevertheless, apart from him and others, she manifests at every moment her constant attendance and her assistance in his pastimes;
and just as it is with Yogamāyā, so it is also with Māyā and the others who follow her.
Even though this is so, Garga has indicated that you yourself must protect him—whose power was granted by your lord—with your own powers, such as your own fortune (*śrī*) and others.
This being the case, his statement, "Thus there will be many names and forms for your son" (BhP 10.8.15), would also be highly appropriate;
for he is one who is possessed by the intense immersion in the rasa of serving those dear to him.

For this very son of the illustrious King of Vraja, who is ever resplendent and who delights in the particular pastimes of the natural disposition of his own affectionate people, a form corresponding to their own nature and appearance manifests and disappears— both near and far— at will, appearing as one and as many.
[102] Then, that very four-armed form which was manifesting within Śrī Vasudeva and Devakī appeared externally;
for, according to the logical principle that the cause is inferred from its effect.
And by that same logic, the two queens of Vraja appeared in their supreme two-armed forms.
This is understood by following the words of Garga, who had undertaken ascetic practices: "Previously, this son of yours was born somewhere to Vasudeva" (BhP 10.8.14).
When, out of fear of the cruel Kaṃsa, Śrī Devakī’s desire arose to manifest her two-armed form while concealing her manifested four-armed form, [the Lord appeared].

Then, that very same unprecedented two-armed form of his which had previously entered the interior of Śrī Yaśodā along with Māyā, having attained presence there, manifested himself by internalizing his four-armed form;
wherein Māyā, though remaining within the mother’s womb in embodied form, became his vehicle through her bodiless upward movement.
The row of nostrils, like the petal of a blue lotus, brought him there entirely unnoticed;

she who, previously, by her attraction for him and her boldness, had even caused her mother to wither with infatuation. Then, moreover, by that form while remaining in the womb, having spread the delusion of her mother’s birth, she enveloped herself within and remained lying upon the very bed of birth.
Indeed, even when Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa was transferred from Śrī Devakī to Śrī Rohiṇī, he proceeded in that same manner.

At this point, Snigdhakaṇṭha thought within himself: "He has surely spoken the truth, for the Blessed Lord had previously declared to Māyā: 'Then I shall indeed go with a portion of Myself' (BhP 10.29). Thus, she was commissioned by the Lord with a portion of Himself for the sake of His purpose.
And the statement "He will come into being" (BhP 10.1.25) is the word of Brahmā addressed to the gods.
Here, the intention of the Blessed Lord is that [He will appear] by means of a partial manifestation (*aṃśabhāga*) in a four-armed form, distinguished by His physical appearance.

The intention of Brahmā is that for the sake of the task at hand, in order to delude those respective [demons], He will come into being with a portion, merging with Śrī Kṛṣṇa in a two-armed form, distinguished by His physical appearance.

Thus, this has indeed been explained elsewhere by those who know the truth of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam regarding the verse: "Balarāma and Keśava descended to the world for its welfare through their own portions" (BhP 10.38.32), where "through their own portions" means "by way of a distinction of forms.

Moreover, the manifestation of Yogamāyā in Kṛṣṇa which was described as being bound by His relationship with the illustrious Queen of Vraja attains full establishment even from the perspective of the final conclusion (siddhānta).
Indeed, the manifestation of all the Blessed One’s powers follows only the desire of those dear to him, and not by chance.
Then, everyone said with wonder: "Let that be so;
however, what happened immediately after that?"

Madhukaṇṭha said: Subsequently, as his manifestation of four arms became manifest through the power of his yoga-māyā, and in accordance with his previous instructions, Śrī Vasudeva— out of fear of the former gods when the illusory sleep had occurred everywhere—
brought this two-armed boy from there and united him with that girl.

However, by means of that four-armed form which indicates His lordship and by His teaching, He did not manifest His state as a son there, and thus Vasudeva remained doubtful regarding His being his son.
But here, by means of the two-armed form and due to the absence of the manifestation of powers such as speech, He manifested that very state and confirmed Him as his son.
The illustrious Ānakadundubhi (Vasudeva), however, did not reflect upon all of this.
Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "Let it be that he does not acknowledge her;

nevertheless, since he himself took away that daughter of this place after disregarding her, and because there was no true intention even in returning her, how could he have accepted her as his own once she had been cast aside?
Even in the scriptures and other sources, his names—such as Nandanandana, Nandātmaja, Nandaja, Nandatanaya, Ballavīnandana, and so forth—are specified as bestowing various desired objects."
[109] Again, he said with a smile: "Even for one who recites the name 'Nandanandana' in reverse, it is experienced as having its syllables inverted;
therefore, even in this way, it is understood that the name is rightly obtained by our king himself, as it directly brings about a fitting birth (*sañjana*) previously indicated.
[110] Having laughed, he spoke again: "Now, let the manner of Vasudeva’s arrival—the son of the god-like lord of Vraja—be described."
Madhukaṇṭha said:
The bond at his feet was shattered, the people lay prostrate, and the barriers at the gates were torn asunder;
the serpent Śeṣa became a parasol, and the river born from the sun reached the state of a mere puddle in a field.
From the house of Āgopādhīśa until Gokula became devoid of fences, having attained the son of Śrī Śūra as its protector—tell me, who owns all this here, and what is it? Speak of that!
[112] Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "All that is the good fortune of the king of the cowherds.
[113] Thus, while this story was gaining renown through their conversation, which was like the spreading of a net of illusions—
When that pastime of Hari indeed entered her eyes as if they were her own,

then at every step there arose states such as the obstruction of tears and the dissolution of facial expressions; how many of those various conditions of the residents of Vraja could possibly be described?

[115] Then, after Śrī Vasudeva had departed having deposited that treasure of jewels, and after Māyā had withdrawn her illusion— which had caused the exhaustion of sleepiness due to the lack of a cause— the wife of the King of Vraja saw her son born once again, manifest before her very eyes.
As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
And having awakened, Yaśodā beheld her newborn son, dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus, and thereupon she attained exceeding joy. (ViP 5.5.22) And likewise:
Candrājit beheld the Child, whose body was like a divine and super-divine dark-blue gem, whose face was like the moon,
whose lotus-eyes transcended the world, and whose hands and feet possessed a beauty surpassing the fresh petals of the celestial tree;
he beheld him who deludes the universe with his cries, sweetened by the softness of his slightly trembling hands and other limbs.
Beholding her son, the queen of the cowherds then considered herself to be like a painting.
"It is the empire of dark-hued splendors, a treasury of jewels of beauty, the fortune of those possessing loveliness, and the manifestation of the Vedas regarding the various rows of her limbs"—
while the beloved of the Lord of Vraja remained thus reflecting, [the sun rose].
Crying out "Om! Om! in this manner, that nine-day-old infant certainly took possession of it.
Upon seeing her newborn son, that mistress of Vraja’s lord was so overwhelmed that she could not even summon her friends; let alone perform any other action,
for her throat and eyes were choked with tears, and her body remained paralyzed.
And therein, due to being under the sway of a longing for fondling, he was distracted by himself through himself.
Furthermore:
When the illusion had vanished, then the people in Vraja abandoned their delusion;
indeed, this occurred at the very moment the glorious Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama) appeared there.
Then, as if revealing the hearts of even those separated from him,
the cool-rayed moon manifested the multitude of blossoms of the night-lilies.
That boy did not appear at all upon his mother’s bed,
like a reflection in the hearts of even the affectionate when they are clear.
Whenever that boy throbbed with life even while hidden from them,
they would then hasten toward him, like female deer at the arrival of the clouds.
The boy was gazed upon by these women, Rohiṇī and the others,
from all sides, like the rising full moon by female cakora birds.
Then, even while she was gazing at her son with smiling eyes from the pillar,
they reflected upon her as one who must be countered and deliberated upon.
Although this child was perceived by her mind’s eye and yet remained unafraid, she repeatedly brought him to a state of doubt; however, that is considered appropriate.
For whatever object is renowned for being extremely difficult to obtain, that is surely obtained through destiny.
However, this [notion] is not at all capable of establishing itself as the first step upon the path of realization.
For example:
"Is this a garland of fresh blue lotuses? Or is it a great sapphire of Śakra? Or perhaps it is lapis lazuli? Alas, this is incomparable, such that it cannot be identified."
Indeed, we behold the body of this child, which, while obstructing the activity of all the senses,
truly extends a state of non-duality to our pair of eyes.
And there—[he was] as if perfumed with the essence of musk and tamāla leaves;
as if anointed with the loveliness of all the *vilambakas*;
as if rubbed with the splendor of his own body.

Having reflected upon that newborn child as one who was, as it were, bathed by the nectar of the luster issuing from his own face; who was, as it were, anointed with the auspicious splendor obtained from the friction of the camphor of his mother’s gaze; and who was, as it were, adorned by his own form suffused with innate beauty.

Having met with one another in secret, they all once again beheld that boy, whose tender limbs were like a deer-marked by the paste of the essence of musk and the decorative patterns of tamāla leaves;
whose hair was as if ground to powder by their own hands; and who, holding his moon-like face, seemed to clench his fists as if to draw in the hearts of all.
They beheld him moving his lotus-like hands and feet like the waves of the river-born Gaṅgā;
and having seen this,
they all, filled with joy, raised a great clamor.
While they were acting thus, they did not perceive what was to be done there;
but one among them, whose mind was exceedingly firm, quickly saw him as he held his two trembling hands.

[120] And then, having immediately recognized the signs of male offspring, she fulfilled each of their desires as follows: "Oh! I shall bear him upon my head; I shall repeatedly touch him with my eyes;
I shall bestow him abundantly upon my heart; I shall cause him to enter the very center of my soul."
Having completely transcended this manifold world of becoming, he was forcibly brought within the range of the vision of those with excellent sight by the power of their gaze.
And there—
repeatedly exclaiming, "Alas! My son has gone from my sight," she was not satisfied even as she wept out of her distress.
Ghana-ruci bestowed upon her a rain of nectar born from the pair of her mother’s breasts, as well as that produced by his very glance.

[121] Then, as all were made attentive through the performance of the festival rites such as the ritual bathing of the Arhat and the child, Rohiṇī, following the command of her husband, approached Nanda with incomparable joy to inform him of the welfare of her son and daughter-in-law.
From the blossoming of her mouth, like white hair curling from the sky, there emerged with speed a radiance of pure luster that rivaled the renown of the smile of the Lord of Light.

[122] Then, when this discourse had reached its conclusion, the members of the assembly—having attained a state of wonder at those various occurrences—stood with palms joined in reverence; and of the two, Madhukaṇṭha and Snigdhakaṇṭha, Madhukaṇṭha spoke:
"O Lord of Vraja, this is that son of yours, who brings about such a wondrous abundance in this assembly."

and when they had arrived, he placed his lotus-like hand upon their heads and adorned them with his own ornaments.

"Today, let lodging be provided for the sake of food and other necessities.

Although the individual soul (jīva) alone occupies the status of the enjoyer, it nevertheless repeatedly desires the expansion of enjoyment for each of its own respective senses, such as the eyes, even while raising both ears with an intense longing to experience [objects] today.
And thus Snigdhakaṇṭha said: Then that aged woman, overflowing with joy, arrived at the cow-pen for the purpose of milking the cows, where the illustrious Nanda, Upananda, and others were stationed;
and there, her gait faltering yet sweet with delight, she beheld them before her.

With joy, he spoke: "Let herds of cows, hastening with speed for the sake of milking here, be released quickly to go to their respective homes without leaving anyone behind.
Then, everyone, out of pride in their delight, said: "Whatever else may be beneficial or desired for her [should be done]. And so—
"Was this boy born together with such joy? Is he indeed that very same one?"—Nanda’s discerning intellect was not capable of distinguishing in this way.

[11] Then the illustrious Lord of Vraja, having assumed the attire of a religious student (*dhārmika*), resolved to give away not only his own abundant wealth but also that of others, such as Bāhula and so forth,
so that everyone might likewise become impoverished.

Having made this resolve and while he was preparing to go home— his desire fulfilled and his dress adjusted— the two great kettledrums resounded from the gateway of the palace at the command of Śrī Rāma’s mother, as the Lord of Vraja, surrounded by various attendants, stood there.

And that music, manifested by those skilled in the science of instrumental arts, clearly proclaimed again and again: "The Joy of Nanda has appeared! Furthermore, at night, the sound of the thundering celestial instruments was heard crying out, "Victory! Victory!", yet the specific cause was not determined.
Then, as they perceived that [event] being recounted, a continuous clamor of joyful shouts arose repeatedly from these living beings of Vraja.

[12] Then, although his body was repeatedly seized by paralysis due to joy, and although he was as if drawn away by longing toward her who had attained a state of trembling, the King of Vraja proceeded toward his own abode, maintaining his composure as if supported by the hand of Lord Nārāyaṇa through his own performed service. And then—
As that herd approaches the dwelling, the groups of kinsmen run forward, meeting one another in succession;
they are like the various cascades following the flow of the Ganges' waterfall.
Just as they bring about growth by being repeatedly rubbed with that very [cloth].
Then the women of the city arrived before him by the thousands, possessing tens of millions of auspicious qualities;
they greatly delighted the Lord of Vraja as he was victorious.
We celebrate with great joy the festival of the birth of the son of Navātman.
Then, accompanied by those in Vraja who were raising a great clamor, the illustrious Lord of Mahā-vraja went forth;
his own beautiful limbs, adorned with ornaments, shone resplendently.
The Lord is like the full moon in the assembly hall of the sky.
Although all the Brahmins had themselves made efforts to come immediately,
nevertheless, for the sake of showing him respect, [he acted as follows].
First, they were summoned individually by the king.
There, filled with joy, he sat amidst that assembly of most affectionate men who were seated sweetly around him, enveloped by an abundance of happiness,
while the best of the brahmins recited Vedic benedictions appropriate for his sons.
He was honored with ease as they placed dūrvā grass and other offerings upon his head.
I praise that very birth of the illustrious and great-souled Nanda, at which he shed his former body with affection and the news of his well-being was heard; I praise nothing else,
for even today, alas, all people clearly attain [liberation] through the mere hearing of it.
Even bathing and other such acts, which yield the fruit of hospitality, do not reach its limit anywhere.

[13] Then, having been instructed by his elders that the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) ought to be performed, he carried it out in such a way as to invert it: "The mothers who were then worshipped by the Lord of Vraja—whose mother was like whom? Thus did the meaning become clear.
Then the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha was prepared by Gopālapāla,
in which the ancestors themselves attained the state of being *nāndīmukha*.

[14] Then, having entered the inner apartments together with those experts in Vedic rites, and having sat upon the foremost altar of the delivery chamber— which was distinguished by auspicious jars and other such items—
the most illustrious lady of the Vraja clan, Rohiṇī, who had ascended her supreme desire, took note of that and, having concealed Yaśodā’s bed— which bestows glory upon the three families—
behind a curtain and covered the infant, she brought him to the threshold of the house.
However, out of joy and playfulness, the matrons, for the sake of their own ornaments, requested this or that thing of priceless value from him in order to see the newborn boy;
yet, when it was promised, they beheld him.

And he indeed possessed a mass of beauty difficult to surpass even by the lord of the multitude of fresh blue lotuses, which are powerful in their state as they circle the world with no small radiance; he was a resting place for rare, soft, and stainless splendor.

His every limb surpassed in excellence the likeness of a stainless blue *cintāmaṇi* gem fashioned by Viśvakarman—the master artisan of the universe—through his efforts to grasp the very essence of all marvelous works;

his mass of soft, smooth, and curly hair was as beautiful as the young moss growing in the clusters of the waters of the Yamunā’s pool, which remained still at its base though its surface was covered with lovely collyrium-like darkness crushed by the forceful current;
and his pure eyes were like the petals within a white lotus shimmering upon the sprout-like hands of Lakṣmī, her abode.

Beholding the child— who possessed hands, feet, and lips that surpassed the tender sprouts of the most excellent wish-fulfilling tree situated in Vaikuṇṭha; who was radiant with the covering of yellow garments, pure and possessing the luster of molten gold, and who was himself the source of delight— he bathed his own self with the water of tears from his eyes and remained for several moments in a state of wonder,
as if drenched in liquid.
Although many kinds of emotions arose in the Lord of the Cowherds,
nevertheless, a powerful dullness was born in him whose nature is profound composure.

[16] Then, after long maintaining her steadfastness, the earth of Vraja— possessing royal splendor, longing for the joy of that [child], and being the wife of Upananda— placed the newborn Nandana upon her lap;
while the sovereign of Vraja bore the infant upon his own lap.
From afar, the Queen of Vraja stood by the bed where her offspring lay; her body rendered helpless by tears born of hearing that news, and by horripilation, paralysis, and other such reactions.
[17] Then, he performed there the rite for generating intelligence, known by the name *śarmānta*,
wherein, having recited "bhūs tvayi" and so forth, the child was made to lick a drop of clarified butter with his ring finger covered in gold.
Thereafter, the rite for longevity (*āyuṣya-kriyā*) was performed.
There, the child was touched with the mantra beginning "Oṃ divaspati," and the ground was consecrated in the four directions and in the center with the mantras beginning "Oṃ hṛdam annaṃ prāṇāya.
Then, the infant was again stroked with the mantra beginning "Oṃ aśmā bhava."

Then, her mother is consecrated with the mantra beginning with "oṃ iḍāsi. Furthermore, the mother's two breasts are washed in sequence with the two verses beginning with "oṃ imaṃ stanam" and "oṃ yas te stanam."

Then, having laid him supine upon the birth-bed, a water-vessel was placed at the region of his head with the mantra beginning "Oṃ āpo deveṣu... and so forth. Thus, when the auspicious *jātakarman* rite had been completed and the time for cutting the infant's umbilical cord had arrived, that very nurse—who had until then been mostly inattentive due to an abundance of supreme bliss—became alert at that moment, her body bristling with horripilation as she took charge of him.
"O King, she announced three or four times, 'This is wonderful!
"Elsewhere, in the lake of her navel, only the stalk (*nāla*) is visible, but not the lotus flower (*nālīka*)."
Furthermore, here it is "nālīka" (lotus) indeed, and not "nāla" (stalk).
Moreover:
his two feet are adorned with the manifest and wondrous marks such as the lotus, the thunderbolt, and the discus.

O Lord of Śrī-Vraja, behold the bodily posture of this child, who possesses the luster of a rain cloud and the majestic splendor that transcends the ocean; he is illuminated by those two hands and by certain other limbs, bestowing wonderful wonders upon us.
[19] And then, while everyone was bewildered by his astonishing conduct, the young students, with a display of laughter, said:
"O Bestower of All Happiness! How can you, whose nature is stainless dharma, justify such a thing as impurity?"

thus, with his moon-like face blooming as all his body hairs bristled with joy, having approached the site of the external fire-oblation surrounded by a multitude of young students, he experienced perfect universal bliss, while the most peaceful root of those various events was offered to his companions.
The illustrious Nanda, having summoned those Brahmins worthy of gifts, prepared for the commencement of the distribution;
he began to give,
yet he could not equal the weight of their company.
By whom such news concerning the glory of his birth was spread everywhere.
Nevertheless—
starting from ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and a million— it reaches ten million;
Nanda gave away as many as twenty lakhs of cows at that point.
Having given two million cows whose horns were adorned with gold,
his heart remained unsatisfied and he desired to bestow them upon another.
He gave away seven mountains made of sesame seeds, each weighing ten *droṇas*;
the twice-born considered the weight of the jewels and gold used for their enclosures to be even greater than that.
And by that sacrificial gift which was bestowed upon those worthy recipients by him,
even as it remained inexhaustible, the eyes of others were brought to a state of wonder.
At that time, there was no familiarity with the countless Bābhravyas; rather, it was their spiritual luster alone that served as their distinguishing mark.

[21] There, those Brahmins who had understood the intent of the Vedas and excelled in their respective branches of learning; the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, bards, *kṛśāśvis*, and singers; and the instrumentalists who played various instruments at will—all of them, gathered together for that festival, made auspicious sounds. Though they were distinct individuals, their voices seemed as if they were not separate, and they filled the world with wonder. Such was the event that took place.
At that moment, even the land of Vraja appeared as if thrilled, how much more so those dwelling in Vraja;
for, through its being thoroughly infused [with joy], it was as if free from distraction, and through its being well-sprinkled, it was as if moist with affection.
It was as if dancing with its moving banners and flags;

and there, even among the cows, bulls, and calves, their natural affection and tenderness were manifested outwardly under the pretext of being smeared with turmeric melted in oil, while the diversity of their joy was revealed through various minerals, peacock feathers, garlands, and golden necklaces.
How much more so, then, for the cowherds, who even today exist by virtue of their fame and are thus called "the protectors of the earth-cows" (gopṛthivīpātāraḥ);

for they have indeed become inseparable from the poetic compositions that describe them, through the manifestation of their aesthetic sentiments (rasa-bhāva) and the employment of poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra).
By holding various offerings made of jewels in their hands as an expression of joy, they manifested both their own affection and their heroism.

And when the cowherds were thus acting, how much more, then, can the excellent wives of the cowherds be described—those who are the mistresses of the clan of Gokula, which was being restored to life, and whose tender hearts were saturated with the multitude of her virtues?
[22] Indeed, they were those who previously, due to the absence of obtaining such offspring, had almost abandoned their ornaments out of a sense of despondency.

But now, upon merely hearing that his offspring was somewhat inclined toward his feet, they experienced various transformations of joy; and for the sake of pleasing him on this festive occasion, they accepted the necessary preparations even if they required delay, and set out toward his city as if dancing.

And because they were accompanied by auspicious signs intended to be manifested, and because they were the fruition of affectionate desires, they themselves carried in their hands offerings made of great jewels.
From their joy, a splendor quite distinct [from that of others] manifested;
for instance, the radiance of these women’s moon-like faces shone forth, surpassing even saffron.
On the festival day of his son's birth, Śrī Yaśodā rejoiced with her husband.

On the road, various garments were arranged in a state of agitation, and the ground was strewn with fallen garlands.
With cheeks framed by swaying jeweled earrings,
and with the edge of her upper garment slipping unnoticed;
With a shimmering complexion as her flickering food,
and variegated garments as her girdle and waist-cloth.
"Overcome by their mutual lack of understanding,
they and their retinues laughed at one another here.

thus were the musical instruments sounded by the deities presiding over those instruments.
From that mass of bliss, preceded by Upananda,
those profound cowherds also sported, danced, and sang.
Then the women who had come there, having gazed upon the child with constant blessings and described him to one another, sang this:
Protect us for a long time, O prince of the Vrajas;
we are but children here, so delicate. (Dhruva)
May you, who have attained swift growth and prosperity,
bring about well-being through that which is desired by you.
We long for you with your smiling face, and for the bliss of your playful movement in the embrace of women.
Your unhesitating movement, hanging from the rows of cow-tails, sways as you turn.
When, alas, will you delight me with the pleasure of wandering among the young calves?
The wandering and roaming of herds of cows belongs to him;
indeed, he who possesses such fortune shall behold this.
To the one who possesses excellent strength, like a fine plantain tree that has cast off its husk; to the one whose fruit is distinguished by the bees of the world’s remaining [beings].
Thus, those beautiful women, skilled in song and possessed of great splendor,
went outside, repeatedly sprinkling themselves with yellow oil.
And then—
sprinkled with curds, milk, and other offerings, these excellent cowherds attained a mutual whiteness and danced like waves of the ocean of milk.

"Behold, O circle of friends, the King of Gokula, who partakes in playful sport following the festival of his son! (Chorus)

From time to time, he gives rare gifts;
as he bestows them and maintains them, he inspires wonder.

this is not the spreading of a mass of butter, but pearls released from the clouds;

[29] Thereupon, the illustrious King of Vraja, bestowing gifts with delight, filled the ocean of his circle of kinsmen.

And having understood that Ānanda was keeping watch over her, they remained truly awake throughout the night, which was blessed with dancing, singing, and other festivities.

Having bound you, I shall quickly depart for home;
if you have the power, display it and commit another theft.
[In the Vasantatilakā meter] [30] Annoyed by her persistence in the effort to bind [him], the son, as if hissing with tears, spoke loudly:

Where have you gone, along with your innate nature?
This [world] binds me who am bereft of you; therefore, come here quickly!

[31] This was not perceived by her as she had gone far away; however, other women from nearby dwellings, having perceived it through hearsay and having engaged in reproachful conduct, gathered together and surrounded her.

Consequently, even when she was seen remaining in that same state after being removed from the braid of hair and placed upon another woman, the Queen of Vraja did not reach the end of the churning, despite many eyes of the women being fixed upon her with wonder. And so—

Within that space measuring two finger-breadths, all the banyan trees appeared to have found room; they were seen there like dense clouds upon Mount Vidūra. Seeing this, the women said with smiles of amusement: [The verse: *In that space appearing to be only two finger-breadths wide, all the banyan trees were seen to have found their place, like thick clouds upon the distant mountain.* [Prose: As they watched this, they spoke thus while laughing.
O Queen of Vraja,
we have already informed you:
this very thief, who delights in the mere pleasure of a small bundle of stolen goods and who even tosses aside a water-jar due to his excessive infatuation, is now being set on fire.

Afterwards, having gained joy from striking the pestle against the thick mortar, he— bound indeed by being surrounded solely by children, his faith in mischief intensified— laughing and playing with them, moved that mortar very lightly; and because of their excessive laughter,

But by that playful act which bestowed joy through the very labor of pulling, he did not achieve the satisfaction of loosening the bond with one hand nor with the other.
However, before the city gate, a pair of *yamala-arjunas*—dancing as if whirled by a whirlwind—stood in his path;

[45] Uttering this much with an open throat, that sweet-voiced one, while deceiving them by suggesting that the reason for breaking it was to proclaim the sovereignty of Hari,
announced another reason altogether— [46] then, clearly and suddenly,
out of a longing to wander elsewhere, he went out by the very path connected through its middle.
Because that path was narrow and low, it struck against the mortar.
Then, clearly desiring to break the *vaṭī* (the pestle), he pulled it;
and when it was forcibly dragged out—
The pair of knee-caps, clearly struck together by the clattering sound of the shanks, rolled about in both directions; yet they did not perceive either intelligence, fortitude, deafness, or delusion.
As he advanced toward the cow-pen, he placed the herd of creatures within its enclosure.
(Rucirā) There, that pair—Arjuna and Vajramajjā—was shattered in a wondrous way;
yet, the bond consisting of the persistent attachment born of a mother’s affection remained unbroken. (Anuṣṭubh)
And regarding this, they utter these verses:

[He who] possesses the luster of a dark-complexioned body, bears the sound of tinkling bells, provides a stage for the dance of the *riṅga* bird, and constantly drags the mortar with a variety of harsh, rattling sounds— [to him we bow].

I praise the childhood of the one cherished by the women of Vraja, whose gaze turned back out of curiosity aroused by the *kaṭatkāra* sound produced by the two Arjunas as they flashed against each other.

[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] [49] Now, for half a moment, because of the exceedingly violent flash of those two, the inhabitants of the cowherd settlement, overcome with distress, fell into a swoon and remained so.
Except for the group of children who were in close contact with her,
Mitrāvalī— whose form was as if painted due to her preeminence in the sweetness of those playful movements— did not experience any fear.

nor, out of ignorance or contempt, did he ask the children,

[58] Then, having emerged from these two broken [gates], adorned with bracelets, crowns, earrings, and other ornaments, their radiant bodies glowing and full of vigor, they bowed down and somehow completely delighted him;
thereafter, they set out toward the northern direction.
Having considered this, those who were compassionate regarded it as the mere prattle of fools;
others, however, became filled with minds that could not escape doubt.

[60] Thereafter, in due course, the King of Vraja, having adorned his lap with his young son and accompanied by the people of Vraja who had gathered in groups of one, two, and so forth, followed the Yamunā to perform his daily rites; having bathed there along with him and performed the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) and other ceremonies by the brahmins, he remained right there.

The illustrious King of Vraja, having also summoned his younger son Rāma, partook of the feast together with that son, his heart melting with the affectionate and sweet clamor of the two boys.

After resting for a moment with those two—who were like personified fullness of supreme bliss—and with his mind steadied by such profound comfort from the cooling root of the uśīra plant, he arrived at the cow-pen at the delightful time when the cows returned.

He also had them perform tasks such as milking cows. Having summoned a white cow from the stable that was even whiter than the dwelling itself, he had his two sons— well-fed and accompanied by their peers— drink warm milk, which served as a substitute for sucking at the breast,
and he instructed them there in the art of fashioning leaf-cups.

[64] Then, having returned once more to the palace, while the King of Vraja was enjoying the pleasure of the evening meal in the company of those two, all the authoritative ladies— who were like the very jewels of their own families and who longed for his continuous happiness— approached him together with Rohiṇī and made this representation:
[65] "O King, Kṛṣṇa’s mother has not eaten today."
She does not speak with anyone, and all others likewise behave toward her in that same manner. Vrajarāja, with a sorrowful laugh, said: "What shall we do?"
"Let her, following her own anger, see her own fault for herself.
Then they all, with tears, said,
"Alas!"
She, indeed, being exceedingly delicate both within and without, will wither away from such talk of yours and from the heat.
But the King of Vraja, smiling, asked his son:
"Will you go to your own mother?"
[69] Kṛṣṇa said: "No, no;
rather, I shall cause you to pass from one season to another.
[70] Then the elder queens, who had children, said with a laugh: "Whose breast will you suck?"
[71] Kṛṣṇa said: "I shall drink warm milk that has not been mixed with curds.
[72] They all asked: "With whom will you play?
[73] Kṛṣṇa said: "With my father alone."
"In that way, I shall also cause my brother to go to the forest.
Vrajarāja said, "Why do you not follow your brother's mother?
Kṛṣṇa replied with tears of anger, "She has departed even leaving me behind."
[76] Having heard this, Rohiṇī, with tears in her eyes, spoke softly: "My son, why are you so hard-hearted?
Your mother is suffering."
[77] Kṛṣṇa, as if not hearing this, looked tearfully at his father’s face;
Rohiṇī, however, signaled to Saṅkarṣaṇa to pull him away.
With his hand grasped by him, Kṛṣṇa then fled, casting off that hand, and settled upon his father’s lap.
And being thus, with his neck enveloped by both arms and beholding only her gaze which shed a rain of tears, he remained utterly submissive to her.
But the King of Vraja, perceiving the internal affection for him within his mother, and raising his hand slightly to manifest it, said: "Son, if you speak..."
"In that case, very well, I shall strike her!
But Kṛṣṇa, unable to endure this, paralyzed his hand.
Then the King of Vraja, laughing again, out of his natural affection and with great compassion, considering even the heart of the boy's mother, said: "O son..."
"If your mother were to become like this, what would you do?
Thus he spoke with a mocking smile, employing a word from the *anadhu* class in a sense contrary to its usual meaning.
[80] But Kṛṣṇa, out of childhood nature, constantly longing for his mother with tears,

[81] Then, amidst the general sound of loud laughter, Rohiṇī, ascending to the height of supreme joy, led him into the house; and having entered, he clung to Ambālikā’s neck with both tears and delight.
And then—placing her chin upon her son’s head, she—
With a lowing sound like that of a cow,
her very self melting through the intensity of her weeping, she causes even all those around her to weep. [Svāgatā meter]

[82] Then, having attained some peace through their manifold consolations, her facial radiance slightly manifesting, this illustrious Sumukhā nourished her son with breast milk; and she took her meal together with that first-born son, accompanied by those most beneficial [attendants]. and on that day, Dāmodara was called out by the women of Vraja with playful joy as "this very one who is dark and enchanting."
In this world, who indeed among the wise would be capable of praising Vrajeśvarī, she who is the sustainer of the worlds and the people,
and whose very fraction is Brahmā, Śiva, and even Ramā?
"And he did not equal even a sixteenth part," so says Bādarāyaṇi.

[Upajāti meter] [84] This glorious sound of the drum of his fame, its true significance perfectly articulated by Bādarāyaṇi, wanders throughout the three worlds in verse. For instance: "Not even Viriñci... (BhP 10.9.20), and so forth.
[85] But Śrī-Rāma said to his younger brother, who was full of longing, "Do you remember, brother?"

saying, "And we shall even play there."
[87] Then the narrator spoke the conclusion: "O Gopa-Maheśvara, such a son has been born to you, who even fashioned those two trees as possessing divine devotion to his own. [Anuṣṭubh]
[88] Thus, when this had occurred, they all experienced various stories and various festivals, and then returned each to his own dwelling.
Thus ends the section titled "Dāmodarānumoda" in the *Śrī-Gopāla-Campū*.
The eighth fulfillment.
//8// Now, the ninth fulfillment: Entry into the region of Śrī Vṛndāvana.
[1] Then, on another day, while the assembly was shining brightly, the illustrious King of Vraja questioned him:
"O child Snigdhakaṇṭha,
those two trees in Vraja are indeed like deities because they grant all desires."
Then, what were they like in their previous birth, or from where did they come here, and at present, in what state have they gone?

Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "In the past, having been born from Dhūrjaṭi-mitra and having displayed audacity toward the most eminent of divine sages (devarṣi), we eventually attained devotion to Your Lordship even in our state as trees—through the supreme grace and the restraint imposed by that most eminent of divine sages.
As he manifested his incarnation according to his own will, we remained in the vicinity of that great forest which was Your abode, existing there in the form of twin arjuna trees."
Immediately thereafter, they returned to their own state and became possessed of supreme devotion to the Blessed Lord;
now, however, they remain experiencing the manifestation of the fruits of that devotion.
Vrajarāja said with curiosity: "Tell me the truth."
"Where have they gone now?
[4] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha, lowering his lotus-like face and remaining as if silent, cast a sidelong glance at Madhukaṇṭha.
Vrajarāja said: "Why did you not speak up, as if shrinking back? [5]

[13] The husband said: "If there is a distinction, let it be told. [14] The wife replied:

Just as the eye is an object of suspicion, so too are the ears and other senses. those two, the sons of your brother, having deceived the foster-mothers— who were objects of suspicion— while they were with Yaśodā, who was filled with joy by the arrival of their own kinsmen, the Lord of Vraja, and his virtuous attendants, as well as with Rohiṇī, who had rendered them assistance.

there, they raised a great clamor with their own friends and arrogant attendants.

"Alas! I do not know whether some tree or a riverbank might have given way, being driven by wicked men like a pair of Arjunas; for while I am obstructed by the ripening of my past karma—"
"Go yourself at once!
She went there quickly, her body and mind agitated,
and then called out to Kṛṣṇa, who was on the riverbank with his Arjuna tree broken.

Seeing her son playing excessively with the other children along with his elder brother, she,

"Today is your birth-star; being pure, give cows to the Brahmins.

"And you, having bathed, taken your meal, and being well-adorned, may you enjoy yourself.

It is true that these two, who possess offspring, have been apprehensive regarding their progeny, seeing this stall and its inner chamber as if it were undefiled.

And here, observing the contraction of the King of Vraja, he perceived the side of what was beneficial for his subjects who were merely children: "Since you have spoken thus for the benefit of Vraja, saying 'One must not remain here,' that indeed appears to me to be primarily for the welfare of those who are very young. [Upagīti]
Whatever corruption has arisen here, born of my own innate nature and despite being guarded with successive efforts, what else could remain in this world? // JGc 1.9.6 // [Āryā]

That state which is both to be abandoned and to be approached:
that which is the cause of suffering is to be abandoned, while that which is the treasury of happiness is to be approached. [Upagīti]

That speech, having itself followed its own meaning, was sufficient for the herd of cattle who were devoid of reasoning;
behold how the difference between seeds [yields fruit] even in soil that merely touches upon similarity.
It shall flourish and bear fruit right here, and not elsewhere.

[In the *Prahārṣiṇī* meter: Thus, having informed even the full moon, having obtained her permission, and having placed her at the forefront, let the herd be quickly roused!— this very sound, which nourishes the cowherd settlement by the resonance of the drum, fulfills its own etymological definition.
Thus he spoke by way of illustration;
for "noise" (ghoṣatā) is defined as the state of being the locus of a great sound, such as the clamor and tumult of cattle and even of humans— as when,

On the road, one person runs; another calls out; someone else speaks a reply;

Everyone sings of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood deeds; they shed tears, become motionless, perspire, tremble, experience horripilation, and fall into a change of complexion. [Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter] The cowherd women, having mounted their carts and adorned themselves with new finery, set out.
Out of joy, they sang incessantly of Ānanda, the son of Nanda;
thus: "O son of King Nanda! O Nanda, son of Yaśodā!"

Anointed by the great festival of his birth, he has delighted all who are affectionate toward him. (Dhruva) The poison of women is neutralized by the mere touch [of him]; he is unfamiliar with the faults of calamity;
he is the remainder of the crushing of the cart, the preeminent merit of the cowherd settlement.

O delightful one, whose name has been established, you who are ever-delighting to your beloveds; O you whose limbs tremble, O you who are devoid of passion, yet who have accepted the company of your friends!

O you who delight in releasing the calves, O Yaśodā who grants happiness to the people of Vraja!

The women of Vraja’s city, with joy born from the conviction that He was their own respective sons, and with the doubled splendor of bliss arising from the manifestation of His friendship,
displayed their affection for Him just as before.
Whatever that perfection of his subdued, it shone as if it were he himself.

JGc_1,11.26 // [Śikhariṇī] Even though the other calves born in Vraja were of the same nature as the son of the King of Vraja, it is nevertheless proper to say that they did not suckle at his very same udder.
That [Self] is indeed their locus, possessing their form, their qualities, and their immeasurable activities;
for it has been declared in various places that it is the cause of its own manifold existence as well.
JGc_1,11.27 // [Sragdharā] [36] Thus, when five or six days have been subtracted from that year which is otherwise characterized by loss, then,
following after the kind of affection directed toward Kṛṣṇa, there arises in those children and others a state of being intent upon themselves and others for the sake of Him.
Through his perfect understanding, Rāma was also struck with wonder; after exchanging questions and answers with him and reaching a firm conclusion, he remained there.
However, because of his anger toward his younger brother—who had been tormented by the deception of all those friends—he did not go to the forest with him for five or six days.
Meanwhile, Brahmā, who had arrived there in secret, was suspected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as follows:
Because he comes and goes, looks ahead and behind, as well as to the sides,
covers himself all around, follows every step, wanders about, and turns in circles;
with a stolen object in hand, he gazes suspiciously at the herd of calves and the cowherd boy.

Therefore, it occurs to me that this thief bears a face in every direction. [Śārdūlavikrīḍita] [37] Then Brahmā, perceiving in his mind the mutual non-difference of those moderns and ancients, such as Bāla and others, by means of their forms and other qualities, was struck with wonder; yet, while observing the ancients, he beheld them as being preeminent above all, abounding in a most magnificent and supreme greatness.

[38] Śrīdāma and his friends saw Brahmā; however, because the desire arose in their own minds to bring [their other] friends there, the state of searching for them occurred by chance, and those who were present at that time were included within that group.
[39] Thus, as the lotus-born one experienced various manifestations of power, he became subject to both satisfaction and remorse, resulting in a state of being turned away from speech.
She herself bent down to offer salutation; yet there,
as he was four-faced, each time he lowered one face,
the other faces reached the zenith as they bowed, so that no single direction could ever be fully completed.

Although Brahmā did not rejoice because he had failed to obtain even a single word from her, nevertheless, he found joy in beholding the moon-like face of Hari. And in that place, as if proclaiming it with his four mouths, he—though all-pervading—extended his own consent toward the very path followed by Gokula;
as he himself said:
"That birth here in this forest is some kind of immense good fortune."
"Even in Gokula, she who bathed her limbs in the dust of his feet—
he whose entire life is Lord Mukunda,
the dust of whose feet even today is sought only through the Vedas. [BhP 10.14.34] Thus it is said.
[41] Thus, being rendered speechless by the mass of rays from the hands of the Lord of the Great Vraja, we find no opportunity for further argument; enough, then, with this excessive detail.
[42] Then Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "What was said there by the illustrious Crown Prince of Vraja? [43] Madhukaṇṭha replied with a smile: "Nothing at all."
But at that time, during the moment of praise, Govinda smiled upon seeing him thus praising; he saw something wonderful there.
For if he who has four faces speaks but once, there might arise the delusion that four [separate beings] are uttering those sounds.
[In the *Praharṣiṇī* meter] [44]: But following the praise,
we cowherds are the ones who possess wealth, while you, O Brahmā, are the one who possesses nothing.
"What shall we say to you?"—as if saying this, he spread a smile. (JGc 1.11.32) [Anuṣṭubh] [45] Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "Even while the Creator is restraining you, has anything at all been said?
[46] Madhukaṇṭha said: "Indeed, at the conclusion of the hymn, by means of his own form which is complete in every respect..."

Even when he did not consider the nourishment of satisfaction provided by the children and others who had appeared later, that blessed and glorious Ajita, conquered by the love of his own kin, desired to bring back those very children of Vraja;

at that time, as Brahmā (Viriñci) requested permission with a gesture manifested by joining his palms, the Lord—smiling with a playful reproach for having been thus entreated—granted him leave, saying: "If it pleases your honors..."
"When the command is understood,
I shall then bring those who were previously connected and present.
Thereupon, Viriñci— his own poor policy having been clearly exposed by the sage’s vow, which was formed by his slightly bowed forehead— manifested his status as the agent of the command.

Overwhelmed by the thrill of her intense devotion and agitated by the distress caused by her own offenses, she circumambulated him three times, prostrated many times, and returned to her own home. Śrī Kṛṣṇa, not perceiving even the slightest offense on her part, and observing that those calves remained in their state of hostility as previously ordained and directed by fate, reunited them with the cowherd boys who were in a similar condition.
[49] Indeed, having reflected upon the reversal of time and place for them, this faultless knowledge was manifested by the god Druhiṇa within his body of affection.
This very point has been stated:
"Then, having taken leave of those who were previously situated in his own abode, the Blessed One..."
"He brought his calves to the riverbank as if to his own former friend. Thus they spoke to their friend Kṛṣṇa.
"Welcome to you who have come with such great speed!
Not even a single morsel has been eaten;

"Then Hṛṣīkeśa, laughing, ate together with the children;

From this it is understood that this hide had been made invisible by his yogic power (*yogamāyā*) for such a long period of time exactly as required.

[52] Then, honored with great joy by those very boys— the cowherd children who had been separated from their calves for the duration of a year— he entered the Vraja, which was filled with the prosperity of its herds, accompanied by them;
and as he directed them here and there to turn back the calves that had strayed beyond bounds, he celebrated a festival more unprecedented than any before.
For it has been said:
"With his body variegated by feathers, flowers, forest-dwellers, and minerals, he is enriched by the festive sounds of powerful flutes, leaves, and horns."
"Chanting for the calves, his pure fame sung after by his followers,
and his glances a festival for the eyes of the gopīs, he entered the cowherd settlement.
Thus, having reiterated his names— Nanda’s son from the side of his father, and Yaśodā’s son from the side of his mother— [he entered].
It was proclaimed that his deed was accomplished instantly, even though it had been performed long ago; for instance:
"Today the son of Nanda has slain the serpent and taken away our time"—this is the refrain.
"Today the son of Yaśodā has slain the serpent and taken away our life"— thus [he thought].
Here, the lower lip is a row of bees upon a cloud;

A heavy breath is like the wind from a forest fire;

Thus they performed various exchanges of limbs, most wonderfully imagined,
along with their respective members.
Fashioning themselves after the serpent,

Having entered into the very center of her womb,

Then, out of an abundance of affection, he [beheld] those who were united with him,

Therefore, he then led him outside;

Greater than life itself,

Having heard this, those staying in Vraja reflected:
"How indeed could the desires of these slayers of the virtuous and drinkers of blood ever be fulfilled?"

[55] Thus, when their meeting had been successfully arranged as one permeated with happiness, Śrīvatsavatsa followed his elder brother in the morning, appeased his charming anger born of affection, and having brought them along with a sense of wonder at what was being offered, he led them all together as before.
Thus he began the rearing of the calves.
Then Madhukaṇṭha, as if with astonishment, said for the sake of concluding the matter:
"O leader of the herd, such a son has been born to you!"
Even Brahmā, the leader of the universe, was like a mere village headman before him.

(1.11.34) Thus, after the two storytellers had expanded their narrative among the members of the assembly— who seemed to witness firsthand the various junctures of their playful dialogue— the two, with palms joined in reverence, remained on their respective paths home that very day as they had been before, each pursuing his own cherished desires.
Even while fashioning their own karma, they took that very same expanded pastime into their hearts.
Thus ends the *Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Campū*, titled "The Liberation from Sin and the Sin of Brahmahatyā."
The eleventh is the fulfillment.
